53737.q: What is La Paz known for around the world as a seat of government?
a: It is the highest seat of government
It is the oldest seat of government
It lies right by the sea
53737.e: La Paz lies at about 3600 metres in a valley basin in the Andes. No other seat of government in the world is so high.
53737.m: La Paz is the highest seat of government in the world.

53738.q: Which means of transport forms a large urban network in La Paz and El Alto?
53738.e: The “Mi Teleférico” network links the neighbourhoods on the steep slopes. It is one of the largest urban cable car networks in the world.
53738.m: In La Paz many people go to work by cable car.

53739.q: What is the largest salt flat in the world, in Bolivia, called?
53739.e: The Salar de Uyuni covers over 10,000 square kilometres. After rain, the sky is reflected on its surface like in a mirror.
53739.m: The Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat in the world.

53740.q: What does Bolivia not have, even though it has a navy?
53740.e: In the 19th century Bolivia lost its coast in a war against Chile. Its navy mainly sails on Lake Titicaca and on rivers.
53740.m: Bolivia is landlocked, with no access to the sea.

53741.e: In the 19th century Simón Bolívar led several South American countries to independence from Spain. Bolivia was named after him in 1825.
53741.m: Bolivia bears the name of the freedom fighter Simón Bolívar.

53742.q: What was the Cerro Rico near the Bolivian city of Potosí famous for in colonial times?
53742.e: The Spanish took huge amounts of silver out of the Cerro Rico. Potosí was one of the largest cities in the world at the time.
53742.m: The Cerro Rico near Potosí was a famous silver mountain.

53743.q: Which farm product from Colombia is especially well known around the world?
53743.e: Colombia is one of the largest coffee producers in the world. Its coffee-growing landscape is even a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
53743.m: Colombia is famous for its coffee.

53745.q: Into which ocean does the Orinoco flow?
53745.e: The Orinoco flows into the Atlantic through a wide delta. The delta consists of many river channels and islands.
53745.m: The Orinoco flows into the Atlantic.

53746.q: Which two large South American rivers does the natural waterway Casiquiare connect?
53746.e: The Casiquiare branches off the Orinoco and flows to the Rio Negro, a tributary of the Amazon. This links two huge river systems.
53746.m: The Casiquiare connects the Orinoco and the Amazon.

53747.q: Which German naturalist explored the Orinoco and its link to the Amazon around 1800?
53747.e: In 1800 Alexander von Humboldt travelled up the Orinoco with Aimé Bonpland. His travel accounts made South America's nature known in Europe.
53747.m: Alexander von Humboldt explored the Orinoco.

53748.q: What are the wide grassy plains along the Orinoco in Venezuela and Colombia called?
53748.e: The Llanos are savannahs that are widely flooded in the rainy season. In the dry season they are parched and hot.
53748.m: The grassy plains along the Orinoco are called the Llanos.

53749.q: Why is the Orinoco crocodile so rare today?
a: It was hunted for its skin
It eats only one kind of fish
It can only live in the sea
53749.e: In the past a great many Orinoco crocodiles were killed for their skin to make leather. Today it is one of the rarest crocodiles in the world.
53749.m: The Orinoco crocodile was almost wiped out.

53750.q: The Warao live in the Orinoco Delta. How do they mostly get around there?
53750.e: In the Orinoco Delta there are many channels and hardly any roads. The Warao build their houses on stilts and travel by canoe.
53750.m: The Warao in the Orinoco Delta get around by canoe.

53751.q: What was the name of the famous giant tortoise from the Galápagos that died in 2012 as the last of its subspecies?
53751.e: Lonesome George was the last known Pinta Island giant tortoise. He became a symbol for the protection of endangered species.
53751.m: Lonesome George was the last tortoise of his subspecies.

53752.q: Which two South American countries do not border Brazil?
53752.e: Brazil borders almost every country in South America. Only Chile and Ecuador share no border with Brazil.
53752.m: Chile and Ecuador are the only South American countries without a border with Brazil.

53753.q: Which city was Brazil's first capital, from 1549 to 1763?
53753.e: Salvador was founded by the Portuguese in 1549 and was the capital of the colony for over 200 years. Its old town, Pelourinho, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

53754.q: Which famous rock rises out of the bay in Rio de Janeiro?
53754.e: Sugarloaf Mountain stands at the entrance to Guanabara Bay and is about 400 metres high. A cable car goes up it.
53754.m: Sugarloaf Mountain is the landmark of Rio de Janeiro.

53755.q: What are the simple neighbourhoods in Rio de Janeiro, often built on steep hills, called?
53755.e: Favelas are densely built neighbourhoods that mostly grew up without permission. In Rio many people live in such areas on the hillsides.
53755.m: The simple hillside neighbourhoods in Rio are called favelas.

53756.q: What is the famous staircase in Rio de Janeiro covered with colourful tiles called?
53756.e: From 1990 the artist Jorge Selarón covered the steps with over 2000 tiles from around the world. The Spanish Steps are in Rome.
53756.m: The Escadaria Selarón is a colourful tiled staircase in Rio.

53757.q: Which gentle style of music came about in Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s?
53757.e: Bossa nova combines samba with jazz. The best-known song is “The Girl from Ipanema”, named after a beach in Rio.
53757.m: Bossa nova comes from Rio de Janeiro.

53758.q: Which large forest lies in the middle of the city of Rio de Janeiro?
53758.e: Tijuca Forest is one of the largest urban forests in the world. It was replanted in the 19th century after being cleared for coffee plantations.
53758.m: Tijuca Forest is a huge forest in the middle of Rio de Janeiro.

53759.q: Which European royal court fled from Napoleon to Rio de Janeiro in 1808?
53759.e: When Napoleon's troops occupied Portugal, the royal family fled to Brazil. As a result, Rio de Janeiro was the capital of the Portuguese empire for some years.
53759.m: In 1808 the Portuguese royal court moved to Rio de Janeiro.

53760.q: For which big festival with samba parades is Rio de Janeiro famous?
53760.e: At carnival the samba schools parade through the Sambódromo in magnificent costumes. Tens of thousands watch.
53760.m: Rio de Janeiro is famous for its carnival.

53761.q: Which is the second-largest country in South America by area?
53761.e: After Brazil, Argentina is the second-largest country in South America. Worldwide it ranks about eighth.
53761.m: Argentina is the second-largest country in South America.

53762.q: From which Latin word for a metal does the name Argentina come?
53762.e: “Argentum” is the Latin word for silver. The Spanish conquerors hoped to find a lot of silver in the region.

53763.q: From which country did Argentina become independent?
53763.e: Argentina was a Spanish colony. It declared its independence in 1816, which is why Spanish is still spoken there today.
53763.m: Argentina used to be a colony of Spain.

53764.q: What is the famous opera house in Buenos Aires called?
53764.e: The Teatro Colón opened in 1908 and, because of its acoustics, is considered one of the best opera houses in the world. La Scala is in Milan.
53764.m: The Teatro Colón is the famous opera house of Buenos Aires.

53765.q: Which pope came from Buenos Aires?
53765.e: Pope Francis was born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires in 1936. He was the first pope from the Americas.
53765.m: Pope Francis came from Buenos Aires.

53766.q: Which drink do people in Argentina often drink from a cup with a metal straw called a bombilla?
53766.e: Mate is made by pouring hot water over the dried leaves of a holly plant. It is drunk from a vessel, often a hollowed-out gourd, through a straw with a filter.
53766.m: People in Argentina love drinking mate.

53767.q: Which huge plant often stands alone on the almost treeless Pampas and gives shade?
53767.e: The ombú looks like a large tree, but botanically it is a giant herb. It is a symbol of the Argentine Pampas.
53767.m: The ombú is the shade plant of the Pampas.

53768.q: Which tall ornamental grass with large, feathery flower heads, also seen in Swiss gardens, comes from South America?
53768.e: Pampas grass comes from the Pampas and neighbouring areas. Its flower heads can grow up to three metres high.
53768.m: Pampas grass gets its name from the Pampas.

53769.q: Which throwing weapon made of leather straps with balls did the gauchos use to catch animals?
53769.e: Bolas consist of two or three balls on straps. When thrown, they wrap around an animal's legs.
53769.m: The gauchos caught animals with bolas.

53770.q: What is a large cattle-farming estate on the Pampas called?
53770.e: An estancia is a large estate, often with thousands of hectares of grazing land. Today some estancias also offer holidays for guests.
53770.m: A large farm on the Pampas is called an estancia.

53771.q: Which invention in the late 19th century made it possible to export fresh beef from the Pampas to Europe?
53771.e: From around 1877, ships with refrigeration brought fresh meat across the Atlantic. After that, cattle farming on the Pampas became big business.
53771.m: Refrigerated ships brought the meat of the Pampas to Europe.

53772.q: In which region of South America is the steep granite mountain Fitz Roy?
53772.e: Fitz Roy is about 3400 metres high and lies on the border between Argentina and Chile in southern Patagonia.
53772.m: Fitz Roy is a famous mountain in Patagonia.

53773.q: Who is the name Patagonia said to come from?
53773.e: In 1520 Magellan's men called the local people “Patagones”. The name of the whole region came from this.
53773.m: The name Patagonia goes back to Magellan's voyage.

53774.q: Which animals can be watched especially well off the Valdés Peninsula in Patagonia?
53774.e: In the bays of the Valdés Peninsula, southern right whales give birth to their young. The peninsula is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
53774.m: You can watch whales off the Valdés Peninsula.

53775.q: What is the Southern Patagonian Ice Field?
a: A huge expanse of ice in the Andes
53775.e: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is one of the largest ice fields outside the polar regions. Many glaciers flow down from it.
53775.m: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is a huge expanse of ice.

53776.q: From which country did settlers come in 1865 whose language can still be heard in parts of Patagonia today?
53776.e: Welsh emigrants founded settlements in the province of Chubut. In some places there are still Welsh tea rooms and schools today.
53776.m: Descendants of Welsh settlers live in Patagonia.

53777.q: Which channel near Tierra del Fuego is named after Charles Darwin's ship?
53777.e: HMS Beagle explored this waterway around 1830. Today the city of Ushuaia lies on its shore.
53777.m: The Beagle Channel bears the name of Darwin's ship.

53778.q: Which tree with prickly leaves is Chile's national tree?
53778.e: The Chilean monkey puzzle tree, or araucaria, grows in the Andes in southern Chile. Its seeds were an important food for the Mapuche people.
53778.m: The monkey puzzle tree is Chile's national tree.

53779.q: The Mapuche are an Indigenous people. In which country do most of them live?
53779.e: The Mapuche live mainly in southern Chile and in Argentina. They are Chile's largest Indigenous people.

53780.q: What is Gabriela Mistral from Chile famous for?
a: She was a poet and won the Nobel Prize in Literature
She was Chile's first woman president
She was the first to climb Aconcagua
She was a famous tennis player
53780.e: Gabriela Mistral was a teacher and poet. In 1945 she became the first person from Latin America to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
53780.m: Gabriela Mistral was a Chilean poet and Nobel Prize winner.

53781.q: Which mountain range rises directly east of Santiago de Chile?
53781.e: From Santiago you can see the snow-covered Andes. The Mapocho River, which flows through the city, also comes from them.
53781.m: Santiago de Chile lies at the foot of the Andes.

53782.q: Which character in a novel was inspired by a real sailor who lived alone on an island off Chile?
53782.e: Alexander Selkirk lived alone on an island off Chile from 1704 to 1709. His story inspired the novel “Robinson Crusoe”. Today the island is called Robinson Crusoe Island.
53782.m: Robinson Crusoe Island belongs to Chile.

53783.q: Which active volcano in southern Chile often has a lava lake in its crater?
53783.e: Villarrica is one of Chile's most active volcanoes. You can sometimes see glowing lava in its crater.
53783.m: Villarrica is an active volcano in Chile.

53784.q: Which Chilean island is known for its wooden churches, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
53784.e: Since the 18th century, craftsmen on Chiloé have built churches entirely of wood. Sixteen of them are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
53784.m: The island of Chiloé is famous for its wooden churches.

53785.q: What is the Atacama Desert in Chile especially known for?
a: It is one of the driest deserts on Earth
It is the largest desert on Earth
It is the coldest desert on Earth
It lies in the middle of Africa
53785.e: In some parts of the Atacama it has not rained for years. It is considered the driest desert outside the polar regions.
53785.m: The Atacama is one of the driest deserts on Earth.

53786.q: What is the large facility with dozens of radio antennas at about 5000 metres in the Atacama called?
53786.e: ALMA stands on the Chajnantor Plateau and observes space with 66 antennas. Several countries run it together, including ESO's member states such as Switzerland.
53786.m: ALMA is a huge telescope facility in the Atacama.

53787.q: What can you see early in the morning in the El Tatio area in the Atacama?
53787.e: El Tatio is one of the highest geyser fields in the world, at about 4300 metres. In the cold morning air the columns of steam are especially easy to see.

53788.q: How do people on the coast of the Atacama use the coastal fog to get water?
53788.e: The coastal fog there is called camanchaca. Fine nets catch the water droplets, which then drip into channels.
53788.m: In the Atacama people collect water with fog nets.

53789.q: What is the well-known hiking trail of several days that leads to Machu Picchu called?
53789.e: The Inca Trail follows old Inca paths over passes and past ruins. Because so many people want to walk it, the number of hikers per day is limited.
53789.m: You hike to Machu Picchu on the Inca Trail.

53790.q: In which country does the Urubamba flow past the Inca city of Machu Picchu?
53790.e: The Urubamba flows through the Andes in Peru, far below in the valley of Machu Picchu. Later it flows into the Amazon.
53790.m: The Urubamba flows past Machu Picchu in Peru.

53791.q: Which people built the famous mountain city of Machu Picchu in Peru?
53791.e: The Incas built Machu Picchu high in the Andes in the 15th century. It was probably a country estate of their ruler Pachacuti.
53791.m: Machu Picchu was built by the Incas.

53792.q: In which mountain range is Huascarán, the highest mountain in Peru?
53792.e: Huascarán in the Cordillera Blanca is about 6770 metres high. The Cordillera Blanca is part of the Andes.
53792.m: Huascarán is Peru's highest mountain and lies in the Andes.

53793.q: Which Spanish conqueror defeated the Incas and founded the city of Lima in 1535?
53793.e: In 1532 Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa. Afterwards the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire and Pizarro founded Lima.
53793.m: Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire.

53795.q: How does Lake Titicaca lose most of its water?
53795.e: Because of the strong sun and wind at about 3800 metres, a great deal of water evaporates. Only a small part flows out through a river.
53795.m: Lake Titicaca loses its water mainly through evaporation.

53796.q: Which place of pilgrimage on Lake Titicaca gave its name to a famous beach in Rio de Janeiro?
53796.e: A famous statue of the Virgin Mary is honoured in Copacabana on Lake Titicaca. A chapel to this Madonna in Rio later gave the beach its name.
53796.m: Copacabana beach is named after a place on Lake Titicaca.

53797.e: Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca was an important centre long before the Incas. The “Gate of the Sun”, made from a single block of stone, is well known.
53797.m: Tiwanaku is a ruined city that is older than the Inca Empire.

53798.q: What is special about Bolivia's official languages?
a: Besides Spanish, many Indigenous languages are official
Bolivia has only English as its official language
Portuguese is Bolivia's only official language
Bolivia has no official language at all
53798.e: Besides Spanish, 36 Indigenous languages are official, for example Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní. Bolivia calls itself a “plurinational state”.
53798.m: Bolivia has a great many official languages.

53799.q: Which Colombian city is called the “City of Eternal Spring” because of its mild climate?
53799.e: Medellín lies at about 1500 metres in an Andean valley. It is pleasantly warm there all year round.
53799.m: Medellín is the City of Eternal Spring.

53800.q: What is the most important river in Colombia, which flows into the Caribbean, called?
53800.e: The Magdalena River flows from south to north through Colombia. It flows into the Caribbean Sea near Barranquilla.
53800.m: The Magdalena is Colombia's main river.

53801.q: Why is the Caño Cristales river in Colombia called the “River of Five Colours”?
a: Water plants colour it red, yellow and green
Colourful glass stones lie on the bottom
53801.e: Water plants grow in the clear water of Caño Cristales and turn red at certain times. Together with yellow sand and green algae, the river glows in many colours.
53801.m: Caño Cristales is Colombia's colourful river.

53802.q: For which export is Colombia the world's second-largest exporter after the Netherlands?
53802.e: Roses and carnations grow in greenhouses on the plateau around Bogotá. Many of them are flown to the USA.
53802.m: Colombia exports a great many cut flowers.

53803.q: Which present-day country belonged to Colombia until 1903?
53803.e: Panama broke away from Colombia in 1903 with the support of the USA. Shortly afterwards the USA began building the Panama Canal.
53803.m: Panama was part of Colombia until 1903.

53804.q: What is Angel Falls in Canaima National Park in Venezuela famous for?
a: It is the highest waterfall in the world
It is the highest mountain in South America
It is the largest cave in the world
It is the longest river in South America
53804.e: The water of Angel Falls drops almost 1000 metres from a table mountain. No other waterfall in the world is so high.
53804.m: Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world.

53805.q: Which waterfall plunges from the Auyán-tepui table mountain in Venezuela and is the highest in the world?
53805.e: Angel Falls drops almost 1000 metres. It plunges from the edge of the large table mountain Auyán-tepui.
53805.m: Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world.

53806.q: What is Angel Falls in Venezuela?
a: The highest waterfall in the world
The longest river in the world
53806.e: The water of Angel Falls plunges almost 1000 metres from a table mountain. The Pemón people call it Kerepakupai Merú.
53806.m: Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world.

53807.q: What happened in 1937 when the pilot Jimmie Angel landed on the table mountain above Angel Falls?
a: His plane got stuck in the bog
53807.e: The plane's wheels sank into the soft ground. Angel and his companions had to climb down on foot, which took eleven days.
53807.m: In 1937 Jimmie Angel's plane got stuck on the tepui.

53808.q: What is a tepui, like Roraima in South America?
a: A table mountain with a flat top
53808.e: Tepuis are table mountains with steep walls and a flat summit plateau. Roraima is about 2800 metres high and lies on the border of Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana.
53808.m: A tepui is a table mountain.

53809.q: What is the mouth of the Catatumbo River at Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela famous for?
53809.e: On many nights of the year there are thunderstorms lasting hours over the area. It is considered one of the places with the most lightning on Earth.
53809.m: Lightning flashes over the mouth of the Catatumbo on a great many nights.

53810.e: Venezuela's currency is named after the freedom fighter Simón Bolívar. The country's highest mountain, Pico Bolívar, also bears his name.
53810.m: In Venezuela people pay with the bolívar.

53811.q: On which large river does the city of Ciudad Bolívar in Venezuela lie?
53811.e: Ciudad Bolívar lies at a narrow point of the Orinoco. The city used to be called Angostura, which means “narrows”.
53811.m: Ciudad Bolívar lies on the Orinoco.

53812.q: Why did explorers only reach the source of the Orinoco very late, in 1951?
a: It lies in remote highlands full of jungle
It lies in the middle of a big city
It lies on an island in the sea
53812.e: The source lies in remote, forested highlands on the border with Brazil. A French and Venezuelan expedition only reached it in 1951.
53812.m: The source of the Orinoco was only reached in 1951.

53813.q: Which seabird on the Galápagos Islands proudly shows off its bright blue feet during courtship?
53813.e: During the courtship dance the male lifts its blue feet one after the other. The bluer the feet, the healthier the bird.
53813.m: The blue-footed booby shows off its blue feet during courtship.

53814.q: Which famous list were the Galápagos Islands added to in 1978 as one of the first sites?
53814.e: In 1978 UNESCO put the first twelve sites on its World Heritage List. The Galápagos Islands were one of them.
53814.m: The Galápagos Islands have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978.

53815.q: Which group of islands does the island of Isabela belong to?
53815.e: Isabela is the largest of the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific. It is made up of several volcanoes that have grown together.
53815.m: Isabela is the largest Galápagos island.

53816.q: Which animals are raised at the Charles Darwin Research Station on the Galápagos Islands?
53816.e: The station helps to save the endangered giant tortoises. The young are raised and later released on the islands.
53816.m: Young giant tortoises are raised on the Galápagos.

53817.q: Which idea did Charles Darwin make famous with his book “On the Origin of Species”?
a: Living things change over long periods through evolution
53817.e: In 1859 Darwin showed that species change over many generations. Well-adapted living things are more likely to survive and have more offspring.
53817.m: Darwin made the theory of evolution famous.

53818.q: Which bird on the Galápagos Islands has such short wings that it cannot fly?
53818.e: The flightless cormorant hunts fish by diving and does not need wings for flying. It is the only cormorant in the world that cannot fly.

53819.q: How many states does Australia have?
53819.e: Australia has six states: New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania. There are also territories such as the Northern Territory.
53819.m: Australia consists of six states and several territories.

53820.q: Which is Australia's largest state by area?
53820.e: Western Australia covers about a third of Australia's area. Its capital is Perth.
53820.m: Western Australia is Australia's largest state.

53821.e: Since 1966 people in Australia have paid with the Australian dollar. Before that, the Australian pound was used.
53821.m: In Australia people pay with the Australian dollar.

53822.q: Roughly how many times bigger than Switzerland is Australia?
53822.e: Australia covers about 7.7 million square kilometres, Switzerland about 41,300. That gives about 186 times.
53822.m: Australia's area is almost 200 times that of Switzerland.

53823.q: In which area is the capital, Canberra?
53823.e: Canberra lies in the Australian Capital Territory, a separate federal territory. It is completely surrounded by New South Wales.
53823.m: Canberra lies in its own capital territory.

53824.q: What do the roofs of the Sydney Opera House remind many people of?
a: the leaves of a palm tree
53824.e: The Danish architect Jørn Utzon designed the white, curved roofs. By the harbour they look like billowing sails.
53824.m: The Sydney Opera House has roofs like sails.

53825.q: What is the nickname of the Harbour Bridge in Sydney?
53825.e: Because of its big steel arch, people in Sydney call the bridge “The Coathanger”. It opened in 1932.
53825.m: Because of its shape, the Harbour Bridge is also called the Coathanger.

53826.q: Which city is the capital of Australia?
53826.e: Sydney is Australia's largest city, but not the capital. Canberra was built specially as the capital between Sydney and Melbourne.
53826.m: The capital of Australia is Canberra, not Sydney.

53827.q: What happened in 1788 in the bay of Sydney?
a: The first British convict colony was founded
The first Olympic Games took place
53827.e: In 1788 the “First Fleet” under Arthur Phillip landed at Sydney Cove. The first British colony in Australia was set up there, mainly with convicts.
53827.m: British settlement of Australia began with the convict colony of 1788.

53828.q: In which year were the Summer Olympics held in Sydney?
53828.e: The 2000 Summer Olympics were held in Sydney. In 1956 Melbourne had been the host city.
53828.m: Sydney hosted the Summer Olympics in 2000.

53829.q: What is the Dingo Fence in the Outback, about 5600 kilometres long, for?
a: It protects sheep pastures from dingoes
It marks the border between two states
It guides hikers through the desert
53829.e: The fence is meant to keep dingoes away from the sheep pastures in the south-east. It is considered one of the longest structures in the world.
53829.m: The Dingo Fence keeps wild dogs away from the sheep.

53830.q: Why do many people in Coober Pedy live underground?
a: Because it gets extremely hot there in summer
Because the town lies below sea level
53830.e: In the opal-mining town of Coober Pedy it gets very hot in summer. In underground homes the temperature stays pleasantly cool.
53830.m: In Coober Pedy people live underground to escape the heat.

53831.q: What is a road train in the Outback?
53831.e: Road trains are articulated lorries with two or more trailers. On the long, straight roads of the Outback they carry goods and livestock.
53831.m: A road train is a very long lorry with many trailers.

53832.q: In which part of Australia is Uluru?
53832.e: Uluru lies in the south of the Northern Territory, in the middle of the Outback. The nearest large town is Alice Springs.
53832.m: Uluru is in the Northern Territory.

53833.q: Off the coast of which state does the Great Barrier Reef lie?
53833.e: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along Australia's north-east coast. This coast belongs to the state of Queensland.
53833.m: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Queensland.

53834.q: Where does the Great Dividing Range run?
a: Through the middle of the Outback
Across Tasmania from west to east
53834.e: The Great Dividing Range stretches from Queensland in the north to Victoria in the south. It is Australia's largest mountain range.
53834.m: The Great Dividing Range lies along Australia's east coast.

53835.q: What is the highest mountain on the Australian mainland called?
53835.e: Mount Kosciuszko is 2228 metres high and is part of the Great Dividing Range. This makes it lower than many peaks in the Swiss Prealps, such as the Säntis at 2502 metres.
53835.m: Mount Kosciuszko is the highest mountain on the Australian mainland.

53836.q: Why do the Blue Mountains near Sydney look bluish from a distance?
a: Because of fine oil droplets from eucalyptus trees
53836.e: Eucalyptus trees release fine oil droplets into the air. These scatter the light so that the mountains shimmer blue.
53836.m: The haze from eucalyptus trees makes the Blue Mountains blue.

53837.q: What effect does the Great Dividing Range have on the weather?
a: It keeps rain on the eastern side
It brings snow to the Outback
It protects the east coast from all rain
It causes monsoon winds in the south
53837.e: Moist air from the Pacific drops its rain on the eastern slopes. West of the mountains it is therefore much drier.
53837.m: East of the Great Dividing Range it is damp, west of it dry.

53838.q: What is the part of the Great Dividing Range with ski resorts in Australia called?
53838.e: The Snowy Mountains lie in southern New South Wales. In the Australian winter, roughly from June to September, you can ski there.
53838.m: You can ski in Australia in the Snowy Mountains.

53839.q: Which is the longest river in Australia?
53839.e: The Murray is Australia's longest river. It is about 2500 kilometres long.
53839.m: The Murray is Australia's longest river.

53840.e: The Murray rises in the Australian Alps in the south-east. These mountains are part of the Great Dividing Range.
53840.m: The Murray rises in the Australian Alps.

53841.q: Between which two states does the Murray form the border for a long stretch?
53841.e: On its upper course the Murray separates New South Wales in the north from Victoria in the south. This is like how the Rhine forms part of Switzerland's border.
53841.m: The Murray separates New South Wales and Victoria.

53842.q: In which state does the Murray flow into the sea?
53842.e: The Murray flows through Lake Alexandrina and reaches the sea in South Australia. The mouth is called the Murray Mouth.
53842.m: The Murray flows into the sea in South Australia.

53843.q: What is the longest tributary of the Murray called?
53843.e: The Darling joins the Murray at Wentworth. Together they form Australia's largest river system.
53843.m: The Darling is the longest tributary of the Murray.

53844.q: Why is the Murray-Darling Basin especially important for Australia?
a: A lot of irrigated farming takes place there
The largest gold mines are there
Half of all people live there in big cities
Most of the oil is extracted there
53844.e: Grain, fruit, wine and livestock are produced in the Murray-Darling Basin. A lot of river water is used for irrigation.
53844.m: The Murray-Darling Basin is an important farming region.

53845.q: What, among other things, did Great Britain use the island of Tasmania for in the 19th century?
a: As the capital of the empire
53845.e: Great Britain sent convicts to Tasmania, where they had to live and work. The ruins of Port Arthur are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
53845.m: Tasmania used to be a convict colony.

53846.q: Which people already lived in New Zealand before the Europeans came?
53846.e: The Māori came to New Zealand by boat from Polynesia about 700 years ago. Aboriginal Australians are the first inhabitants of Australia.
53846.m: The Māori are New Zealand's first inhabitants.

53847.q: Which city was the capital of New Zealand before Wellington became the capital in 1865?
53847.e: Auckland was the capital until 1865. Wellington was chosen because it lies more centrally between the North and South Islands.
53847.m: Wellington became the capital in place of Auckland in 1865.

53848.q: What is New Zealand's largest lake, on the North Island, called?
53848.e: Lake Taupō fills the crater of a huge volcano. It is New Zealand's largest lake.
53848.m: Lake Taupō is New Zealand's largest lake.

53849.q: What is the area around Rotorua on the North Island known for?
53849.e: Rotorua lies in a volcanically active area. There are geysers, bubbling mud pools and a smell of sulphur there.
53849.m: Rotorua is known for geysers and hot springs.

53850.q: What kind of mountain is Ruapehu, the highest mountain on New Zealand's North Island?
53850.e: Ruapehu is an active volcano about 2800 metres high. There are even ski areas on its slopes.
53850.m: The volcano Ruapehu is the highest mountain on the North Island.

53851.q: Which of New Zealand's two main islands has more inhabitants?
53851.e: About three quarters of the population live on the North Island. Auckland and Wellington are there.
53851.m: Most of New Zealand's people live on the North Island.

53852.q: What is a famous fjord on New Zealand's South Island called?
53852.e: Milford Sound lies in Fiordland National Park. It was shaped by glaciers and has steep rock walls.
53852.m: Milford Sound is a well-known fjord on the South Island.

53853.q: What is special about the languages in Papua New Guinea?
a: Everyone speaks the same language as in Australia
53853.e: Papua New Guinea is the country with the most languages in the world. So that everyone can understand each other, there is a shared common language.
53853.m: Over 800 languages are spoken in Papua New Guinea.

53854.q: From which country did Papua New Guinea become independent in 1975?
53854.e: Papua New Guinea was previously run by Australia. On 16 September 1975 it became an independent country.
53854.m: Papua New Guinea has been independent from Australia since 1975.

53855.q: With which country does Papua New Guinea share the island of New Guinea?
53855.e: The island of New Guinea is split in two. The east is Papua New Guinea, the west belongs to Indonesia.
53855.m: New Guinea is divided between Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.

53856.e: The Greek word “mikros” means small. Micronesia consists of many very small islands in the western Pacific.

53857.q: Where does most of Micronesia lie?
a: Off the coast of South America
53857.e: Most of Micronesia's islands lie in the western Pacific north of the equator. They include Guam, Palau and the Marshall Islands.
53857.m: Most of Micronesia lies north of the equator.

53858.e: Guam is the largest island of the Marianas and belongs to the USA. The Marianas are part of Micronesia.

53859.e: The Greek word “melas” means black. European seafarers named the region after the dark skin colour of many of its inhabitants.

53860.q: Which large island belongs to Melanesia?
53860.e: New Guinea is the second-largest island on Earth. It lies north of Australia and, like Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands, belongs to Melanesia.
53860.m: New Guinea is the largest island in Melanesia.

53861.q: Which country does the island group of New Caledonia in Melanesia belong to?
53861.e: New Caledonia is a French overseas territory. A lot of nickel is mined there.

53862.q: From which country did Fiji become independent in 1970?
53862.e: Fiji was a British colony and became independent on 10 October 1970. It is a member of the Commonwealth.
53862.m: Fiji has been independent from Great Britain since 1970.

53863.q: Which line runs through the islands of Fiji?
53863.e: The 180th meridian crosses some of Fiji's islands, for example Taveuni. But the date line was drawn so that all of Fiji has the same date.

53864.q: Where did the ancestors of many Indo-Fijians come from?
53864.e: From 1879 the British brought workers from India for the sugar cane fields. Their descendants now make up a large part of the population.
53864.m: Many people in Fiji have Indian ancestors.

53865.q: According to Charles Darwin, how does an atoll form?
a: A volcano sinks while the reef around it keeps growing
A glacier melts in the sea
The wind piles up a sandbank
53865.e: First a reef grows around a volcanic island. The island slowly sinks, the reef grows upwards, and what is left is a ring with a lagoon.
53865.m: Atolls form from reefs around sunken volcanic islands.

53866.q: What is Bikini Atoll known for?
a: For the first Olympic Games in the Pacific
For the largest aquarium in the world
53866.e: Between 1946 and 1958 the USA tested atomic bombs on Bikini Atoll. The inhabitants had to leave their home.
53866.m: Atomic bombs were tested on Bikini Atoll.

53867.q: Why are many atolls threatened by rising sea levels?
a: They lie only a little above the sea
They sink by metres every year because of earthquakes
53867.e: Most atoll islands rise only one or two metres out of the water. If the sea level rises, they are at risk of flooding.
53867.m: Flat atolls are endangered by rising sea levels.

53868.q: What is the shallow stretch of water inside an atoll called?
53868.e: The lagoon is enclosed by the ring of reef and is usually calm and shallow. It often has only narrow passages to the open sea.
53868.m: There is a lagoon inside an atoll.

53869.q: Which language does the word “atoll” come from?
53869.e: The word comes from Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives. There the ring-shaped groups of islands are called “atholhu”.
53869.m: The word atoll comes from the Maldives.

53870.q: Roughly how many people live in Australia (as of 2025)?
53870.e: According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, about 27.6 million people lived in Australia in mid-2025. That is about three times as many as in Switzerland.
53870.m: Almost 28 million people live in Australia.

53871.q: Why was Canberra built as Australia's new capital?
a: Sydney and Melbourne could not agree
Sydney was destroyed by an earthquake
Melbourne was too close to the equator
The Queen of England wanted it
53871.e: Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be the capital. As a compromise, a new city was built between them. Until 1927 parliament met temporarily in Melbourne.
53871.m: Canberra is a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

53872.q: In which part of Australia is Canberra?
53872.e: Canberra lies in south-eastern Australia, between Sydney and Melbourne. There is a large artificial lake in the city.

53873.q: On which ocean does Sydney lie?
53873.e: Sydney lies on Australia's east coast on the Pacific. The city's natural harbour is called Port Jackson.

53874.q: Which town lies roughly in the middle of Australia in the Outback?
53874.e: Alice Springs lies in the south of the Northern Territory, almost at the geographical centre of the continent. The town is an important supply centre for the Outback.
53874.m: Alice Springs is the town in Australia's red centre.

53875.q: What does a large salt lake in the Outback usually look like?
a: Like a dry, white crust of salt
Like a deep blue mountain lake
53875.e: It rarely rains in the Outback. The salt lakes are therefore mostly dried up and covered only by a white layer of salt.
53875.m: The salt lakes in the Outback are usually dry.

53876.q: How do people on remote farms in the Outback get medical help in an emergency?
a: They go to hospital by ship
A doctor lives on every farm
They wait for the next train
53876.e: The farms are often hundreds of kilometres from the nearest town. The flying doctor service lands right next to them in small planes.
53876.m: In the Outback the doctors come by plane.

53877.q: Where do many farms in the dry Outback get their water from?
a: From groundwater brought up through boreholes
From large rivers that flow all year round
53877.e: A huge store of groundwater lies beneath the Outback. Through boreholes the water reaches the surface, sometimes even on its own.
53877.m: In the Outback water is brought up from underground.

a: Iron in the rock has rusted on the surface
It is made of glowing lava
53878.e: Uluru is made of a sandstone that contains iron. On the surface the iron rusts, which is why the rock glows red, especially at sunset.
53878.m: Rust in the rock makes Uluru red.

53880.q: Roughly how long is a circular walk around the base of Uluru?
53880.e: The rock's circumference at ground level is about 9 kilometres. The walking path around it is a good 10 kilometres long.
53880.m: Walking around Uluru is about 10 kilometres.

53882.q: By which English name was Uluru known in the past?
53882.e: In 1873 a British explorer named the rock “Ayers Rock” after a politician. Today the name used by the Aboriginal people, Uluru, is used again.
53882.m: Uluru used to be called Ayers Rock.

53883.q: What is the national park that Uluru belongs to called?
53883.e: The national park includes Uluru and a nearby group of rock domes. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
53883.m: Uluru lies in Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park.

53884.q: In which sea does the Great Barrier Reef lie?
53884.e: The Coral Sea is a marginal sea of the Pacific off Australia's north-east coast. It is named after its many reefs.
53884.m: The Great Barrier Reef lies in the Coral Sea.

53885.q: Which seafarer ran his ship aground on the Great Barrier Reef in 1770?
53885.e: James Cook's Endeavour was badly damaged on the reef in 1770. The crew managed to repair the ship on land.
53885.m: James Cook ran aground on the Great Barrier Reef in 1770.

53886.q: What do tens of thousands of green turtles do on Raine Island on the Great Barrier Reef?
a: They lay their eggs in the sand
53886.e: In some years, tens of thousands of green turtles lay their eggs on the small Raine Island. It is the largest known nesting site of this species.
53886.m: Raine Island is the nursery of the green turtle.

53887.q: What happens once a year during the great coral spawning on the Great Barrier Reef?
a: Many corals release eggs and sperm at the same time
All the corals lose their colour
The corals move into deeper water
The corals are eaten by fish
53887.e: A few nights after a full moon, usually in November or December, many corals release bundles of eggs and sperm into the water at the same time. This makes it easier for the cells to find each other.
53887.m: During coral spawning, many corals reproduce on the same night.

53888.q: In which animals does the clownfish hide on the Great Barrier Reef?
53888.e: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. A layer of slime protects them from being stung.
53888.m: The clownfish lives safely in a sea anemone.

53889.q: According to many sources, what is the Great Barrier Reef?
a: The largest structure on Earth built by living things
The oldest mountain range on Earth
The largest freshwater lake on Earth
The deepest point in the ocean
53889.e: Billions of tiny coral animals have built the reef system over thousands of years. No other structure built by living things is bigger.
53889.m: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things.

53890.q: Which seafarer is Tasmania named after?
53890.e: The Dutchman Abel Tasman reached the island in 1642. He first called it Van Diemen's Land; since 1856 it has been named Tasmania after him.
53890.m: Tasmania is named after Abel Tasman.

53891.q: What is the capital of Tasmania?
53891.e: Hobart lies at the mouth of the River Derwent in the south-east of the island. Sydney, Perth and Darwin are on the Australian mainland.
53891.m: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania.

53892.q: Which country does the island of Tasmania belong to?
53892.e: Tasmania lies south of the Australian mainland and is a state of Australia.

53893.q: Which carnivorous marsupial is named after Tasmania?
53893.e: The Tasmanian devil is a sturdy carnivorous marsupial with a loud screech. In the wild it lives almost only on Tasmania.
53893.m: The Tasmanian devil lives mainly on Tasmania.

53894.q: What is the large World Heritage area in south-western Tasmania called?
53894.e: The Tasmanian Wilderness has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982. It includes temperate rainforest, mountains and wild rivers.
53894.m: South-western Tasmania is protected as the Tasmanian Wilderness.

53895.q: Roughly how big is Tasmania compared with Switzerland?
53895.e: Tasmania covers about 68,000 square kilometres, Switzerland about 41,300. That gives about 1.7 times.
53895.m: Tasmania is a little bigger than Switzerland.

53896.q: Which Indigenous language is an official language in New Zealand?
53896.e: Māori has been an official language by law since 1987, and New Zealand Sign Language since 2006. Most people speak English in everyday life.
53896.m: Māori is an official language of New Zealand.

53897.q: Which British seafarer drew accurate maps of New Zealand's coasts in 1769?
53897.e: James Cook came to New Zealand in October 1769. He sailed around the islands and mapped their coasts very accurately.
53897.m: James Cook mapped New Zealand's coasts in 1769.

53898.q: Roughly how many people live in New Zealand (as of 2024)?
53898.e: New Zealand has a little over 5 million inhabitants. That is clearly fewer than Switzerland, even though the country is more than six times bigger.
53898.m: A little over 5 million people live in New Zealand.

53899.q: What is New Zealand's currency called?
53899.e: The New Zealand dollar was introduced in 1967. It replaced the New Zealand pound.
53899.m: In New Zealand people pay with the New Zealand dollar.

53900.q: On which strait does the capital, Wellington, lie?
53900.e: Cook Strait separates the North Island from the South Island. Ferries sail from Wellington to Picton on the South Island.

53901.q: Who is the city of Wellington named after?
53901.e: The city was named after Arthur Wellesley, the 1st Duke of Wellington. In 1815 he and his allies defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.
53901.m: Wellington bears the name of the victor of Waterloo.

53902.q: Which largest city on New Zealand's South Island was hit by a severe earthquake in 2011?
53902.e: In the earthquake of 22 February 2011, 185 people died in Christchurch. Many buildings in the centre, including the cathedral, were badly damaged.
53902.m: Christchurch was hit by a severe earthquake in 2011.

53903.q: What is special about some glaciers on the west coast of New Zealand's South Island?
a: They reach down close to the rainforest
They lie in the middle of a desert
They are made entirely of salt
They flow straight into the Dead Sea
53903.e: The Franz Josef and Fox Glaciers flow a long way down from the Southern Alps. Temperate rainforest grows very close by.
53903.m: On the South Island glaciers reach almost to the rainforest.

53904.q: Which place in New Zealand is famous for bungee jumping and adventure sports?
53904.e: The world's first commercial bungee jump opened at the Kawarau Bridge near Queenstown in 1988. In winter the town is the starting point for several ski areas.
53904.m: Queenstown is a stronghold of adventure sports.

53905.q: What covers a large part of Papua New Guinea?
53905.e: Papua New Guinea lies close to the equator. A large part of the country is covered by dense tropical rainforest.
53905.m: A lot of tropical rainforest grows in Papua New Guinea.

53906.q: Roughly how many people live in Papua New Guinea (as of 2023)?
53906.e: In 2023 Papua New Guinea had about 10 million inhabitants. After Australia, that makes it the most populous country in Oceania.
53906.m: About 10 million people live in Papua New Guinea.

53907.q: Which European country had a colony in the north-east of New Guinea until the First World War?
53907.e: At that time the north-east was called Kaiser-Wilhelmsland and was part of German New Guinea. In the First World War Australia occupied the area.
53907.m: Part of Papua New Guinea used to be a German colony.

53908.q: Which continent lies south of New Guinea, separated only by a narrow strait?
53908.e: Between New Guinea and the northern tip of Australia there is only a narrow strait with many small islands.
53908.m: New Guinea lies very close to Australia.

53909.q: Which US state lies in Polynesia?
53909.e: Hawaii forms the northern tip of the Polynesian Triangle. It has been a US state since 1959.
53909.m: Hawaii is the Polynesian state of the USA.

a: A world of islands in the Pacific
53910.e: Polynesia includes thousands of islands in the Pacific, such as Hawaii, Samoa, Tahiti and Easter Island.
53910.m: Polynesia is a world of islands in the Pacific.

53911.q: How did the first people reach the islands of Polynesia?
a: By canoe across the open sea
On foot over a land bridge
53911.e: The ancestors of the Polynesians sailed thousands of kilometres in large outrigger canoes. They found their way using the stars, the waves and birds.

53912.q: Which European country does the island of Tahiti still belong to today?
53912.e: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia. This area is an overseas country of France.

53913.q: What is Fiji especially known for among travellers?
53913.e: Fiji consists of over 300 islands in the South Pacific. Warm beaches and colourful coral reefs attract many visitors.
53913.m: Fiji is known for its beaches and coral reefs.

53915.q: Roughly how many people live in Fiji (as of 2022)?
53915.m: Almost a million people live in Fiji.

53916.q: Which part of the world is Fiji counted as part of?
53916.e: Fiji is an island country in the South Pacific. Together with Australia, New Zealand and many other islands, it belongs to Oceania.

53917.q: What is the ring of an atoll made of?
53917.e: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef with a lagoon in the middle. There are often many small islands on the reef.
53917.m: Atolls are rings of coral reef.

53918.q: Which island country in the Indian Ocean is made up of 26 natural atolls?
53918.e: The Maldives consist of 26 natural atolls with over 1000 small islands. Hardly any other country is so flat.
53918.m: The Maldives are made up of many atolls.

53919.q: Which continent has the greatest average height above sea level?
53919.e: Because of its ice, which is over 4 kilometres thick in places, Antarctica lies on average more than 2000 metres high. No other continent is so high on average.
53919.m: On average Antarctica is the highest continent.

53920.q: Roughly what percentage of Antarctica's area is covered by ice?
53920.e: Only a very small part of Antarctica, such as mountain peaks and some coastal areas, is free of ice. The rest lies under the Antarctic ice sheet.
53920.m: Almost all of Antarctica is covered by ice.

53921.q: Where does Antarctica rank among the continents by area?
53921.e: Antarctica covers about 14 million square kilometres. That makes it bigger than Europe and Australia, but smaller than Asia, Africa, North America and South America.

53922.q: What is the southernmost active volcano on Earth, with a lava lake in its crater, called?
53922.e: Mount Erebus lies on Ross Island in Antarctica. In its crater is one of the few permanent lava lakes on Earth.
53922.m: Mount Erebus is an active volcano in Antarctica.

53923.q: Which part of Antarctica reaches furthest north towards South America?
53923.e: The Antarctic Peninsula sticks out like a finger towards South America. It is the warmest part of the continent and is visited by many expedition ships.
53923.m: The Antarctic Peninsula points towards South America.

53924.q: Which mountain range divides Antarctica into an eastern and a western part?
53924.e: The Transantarctic Mountains are over 3000 kilometres long. They separate the large East Antarctica from the smaller West Antarctica.
53924.m: The Transantarctic Mountains divide Antarctica into east and west.

53925.q: Which British polar explorer died with his companions in 1912 on the way back from the South Pole?
53925.e: Scott reached the South Pole in January 1912, shortly after the Norwegians. On the way back he and his companions died in the cold and storms.
53925.m: Robert Falcon Scott died in 1912 on the way back from the South Pole.

53926.q: What happened in 1915 in Antarctica to the ship of the polar explorer Ernest Shackleton?
a: It was crushed by the ice and sank
It was the first to reach the South Pole
It was turned into a museum
It sailed all the way round Antarctica
53926.e: The Endurance was trapped and crushed by pack ice. Even so, Shackleton brought all his men back alive.
53926.m: Shackleton's ship was crushed by the ice in 1915.

53927.q: Which continent was the last to be discovered by humans?
53927.e: Antarctica was only sighted around 1820 and set foot on even later. All the other continents had been inhabited or known much earlier.
53927.m: Antarctica was the last continent to be discovered.

53928.q: Which activity does the Antarctic Treaty expressly promote?
53928.e: The Antarctic Treaty wants countries to carry out research together peacefully in Antarctica. Many countries run research stations there.

a: An agreement between many countries on the peaceful use of Antarctica
A purchase contract by which the USA bought Antarctica
A plan to build a city at the South Pole
A rule that only applies to penguins
53929.e: In the Antarctic Treaty, many countries agreed to use Antarctica only for peaceful purposes. It was signed in 1959.
53929.m: The Antarctic Treaty governs the peaceful use of Antarctica.

53930.q: Which area does the Antarctic Treaty apply to?
53930.e: The treaty applies to all land and ice areas south of latitude 60 degrees south. This includes the whole of Antarctica.
53930.m: The Antarctic Treaty applies south of 60 degrees south.

53931.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty forbid in Antarctica?
53931.e: Antarctica may only be used peacefully; military bases and weapons tests are forbidden. Research is expressly welcome.
53931.m: Antarctica may only be used peacefully.

53932.q: What is true of Switzerland and the Antarctic Treaty?
a: It is one of the parties to the treaty
It owns its own territory in Antarctica
It has a military base there
It is not allowed to set foot in Antarctica
53932.e: Switzerland has been a party to the treaty since 1990. Swiss researchers work in Antarctica on topics such as ice and climate.
53932.m: Switzerland is part of the Antarctic Treaty.

53933.q: Under the Antarctic Treaty, what happens to individual countries' territorial claims?
53933.e: Several countries claim parts of Antarctica. The treaty puts these claims on ice, and new claims are not allowed.
53933.m: The Antarctic Treaty freezes all territorial claims.

53934.q: What may countries in the Antarctic Treaty carry out at other countries' stations at any time?
53934.e: Observers from the treaty countries may visit all stations, ships and facilities at any time. This is to check that the rules are being followed.
53934.m: The Antarctic Treaty allows mutual inspections.

53935.q: Which of these countries is one of the eight member states of the Arctic Council?
53935.e: The members of the Arctic Council are Canada, the USA, Russia, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland. Other countries can only be observers.
53935.m: Finland is one of the eight Arctic states.

53936.q: What status has Switzerland had in the Arctic Council since 2017?
53936.e: Switzerland was given observer status in the Arctic Council in 2017. Swiss researchers study glaciers, snow and climate in the Arctic, for example.
53936.m: Switzerland has been an observer in the Arctic Council since 2017.

53937.q: Why do no trees grow in large parts of the Arctic?
a: The summer is too short and too cold
There is too much rain there
The animals eat all the trees
53937.e: In the Arctic it stays cool even in summer. Trees cannot grow enough there, so there are only mosses, grasses and dwarf shrubs.
53937.m: In the Arctic the summer is too cold for trees.

53938.q: Which large island in the Arctic, almost completely covered by ice, belongs to Denmark?
53938.e: Greenland is the largest island in the world. It belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark and is mostly covered by a thick ice sheet.
53938.m: Greenland is a huge ice island in the Arctic.

53939.q: From which Greek word does the name “Arctic” come?
53939.e: The Greek word “arktos” means bear. It refers to the constellation of the Great Bear, which is in the northern sky.
53939.m: The name Arctic comes from the Greek word for bear.

53940.q: Roughly how much faster than the global average has the Arctic warmed in recent decades?
a: about two to four times as fast
53940.e: When bright ice and snow melt, darker sea or land appears, which absorbs more of the sun's heat. This makes the warming in the Arctic itself stronger.
53940.m: The Arctic is warming several times faster than the rest of the Earth.

53941.q: Which large white owl breeds in the Arctic tundra?
53941.e: The snowy owl is well adapted to the cold and even has feathered feet. In summer it mainly hunts lemmings.
53941.m: The snowy owl is the white owl of the Arctic.

53942.q: How big can the largest icebergs in Antarctica get?
a: As big as a quarter of Switzerland
As big as a football pitch
53942.e: Iceberg B-15 broke off in 2000 and covered about 11,000 square kilometres, more than a quarter of Switzerland.

53943.q: Which organisation was set up after the sinking of the Titanic to warn ships about icebergs?
53943.e: The International Ice Patrol has been watching icebergs in the North Atlantic since 1914. It is run by the US Coast Guard.
53943.m: The International Ice Patrol warns ships about icebergs.

53944.q: Where do most icebergs in the North Atlantic come from?
53944.e: It is mainly the glaciers on Greenland's west coast that release many icebergs. Ocean currents then carry them south into the Atlantic.
53944.m: Most icebergs in the North Atlantic come from Greenland.

53945.q: Why do some icebergs look blue?
a: The ice is very dense and contains hardly any air bubbles.
They are made of frozen sea water with algae.
53945.e: Very dense ice absorbs red light and mainly lets blue light through. White ice, on the other hand, contains many tiny air bubbles that scatter the light.
53945.m: Dense ice without air bubbles glows blue.

53946.q: What happens to sea level when an iceberg that is already floating melts?
a: It rises as much as when a glacier on land melts.
53946.e: A floating iceberg already displaces as much water as it weighs. So when it melts, sea level hardly changes, unlike with ice that lies on land.
53946.m: Melting ice on land raises sea level; floating ice hardly does.

53947.q: Which country runs the largest research station in Antarctica?
53947.e: The American McMurdo Station lies on Ross Island. In summer over 1000 people live there.
53947.m: The largest station in Antarctica belongs to the USA.

53948.q: What lies deep under the ice beneath Russia's Vostok Station?
53948.e: Lake Vostok lies about 4 kilometres under the ice. It is the largest known lake under the Antarctic ice.
53948.m: A huge lake lies beneath Vostok Station.

53949.q: Which country runs Neumayer Station III?
53949.e: Neumayer Station III is run by Germany's Alfred Wegener Institute. It stands on stilts on the Ekström Ice Shelf.
53949.m: Neumayer Station III is a German station.

53951.q: What is the Belgian Princess Elisabeth station known for?
a: as the first station that runs without CO2 emissions
as the oldest station in Antarctica
as the only station at the South Pole
as the largest station in Antarctica
53951.e: The Princess Elisabeth station opened in 2009 and gets its energy from wind and sun. It is considered Antarctica's first zero-emission station.
53951.m: The Belgian station runs on wind and solar power.

53952.q: Which Swiss organisation has been promoting polar research since 2016?
53952.e: The Swiss Polar Institute was founded in 2016. It supports Swiss researchers in the Arctic, Antarctica and high mountains and organised an expedition around Antarctica.
53952.m: The Swiss Polar Institute promotes Swiss polar research.

53953.q: Why do some research stations in Antarctica stand on legs with skis?
a: So they do not sink into the snow and can be moved
So they can float in summer
53953.e: The ice is always moving and new snow keeps falling. That is why the British station Halley VI stands on legs with skis; in 2017 it was towed to a new site.
53953.m: Some Antarctic stations can move on skis.

53954.q: Roughly how many people live in Greenland (as of 2025)?
53954.e: Only about 57,000 people live in Greenland, most of them on the coast. That is fewer inhabitants than the city of Lucerne.
53954.m: Greenland is huge but has only about 57,000 inhabitants.

53955.q: Which language has been Greenland's only official language since 2009?
53955.e: Since self-government in 2009, Greenlandic, also called Kalaallisut, has been the official language. Danish is still widely used, however.
53955.m: In Greenland, Greenlandic is the official language.

53956.q: Which kingdom does Greenland belong to?
53956.e: Greenland belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark but largely governs itself. In Greenlandic it is called Kalaallit Nunaat, “land of the people”.

53957.q: Which Viking gave Greenland its name in the 10th century?
53957.e: Erik the Red called the land “Greenland” to attract settlers. Around 985 Vikings founded the first settlements there.
53957.m: Erik the Red gave Greenland its name.

53958.q: Why did Greenland leave the European Community in 1985?
a: It wanted to control its own fishing
It did not want the euro
It wanted to be allowed to sell oil
53958.e: After a referendum in 1982, Greenland left the European Community in 1985. One important reason was control over its own fishing.
53958.m: Greenland left the European Community in 1985 because of fishing.

53959.q: What is special about Gunnbjørn Fjeld, Greenland's highest mountain?
a: It is the highest mountain north of the Arctic Circle
It is higher than Mount Everest
It is completely free of ice
53959.e: Gunnbjørn Fjeld on the east coast is about 3700 metres high. No mountain north of the Arctic Circle is higher.
53959.m: Gunnbjørn Fjeld is the highest mountain in the Arctic.

53960.q: Which record does the national park in north-eastern Greenland hold?
a: largest national park in the world
oldest national park in the world
smallest national park in the world
53960.e: Northeast Greenland National Park covers almost a million square kilometres. That makes it bigger than most countries on Earth.
53960.m: The largest national park in the world is in Greenland.

53961.q: Which part of the economy is most important for Greenland's exports?
53961.e: Fish and seafood such as prawns and halibut make up most of the exports. Farming is hardly possible because of the climate.

53962.q: On which date does Greenland celebrate its national day?
53962.e: Greenland celebrates on 21 June, the longest day of the year. Switzerland, on the other hand, celebrates its national day on 1 August.
53962.m: Greenland celebrates its national day on the longest day of the year.

53963.q: Roughly what part of Greenland's area is covered by the ice sheet?
53963.e: The Greenland ice sheet covers about four fifths of the island. The ice-free parts are mainly strips along the coast, where people also live.
53963.m: About four fifths of Greenland lies under ice.

53964.q: Roughly how thick is the Greenland ice sheet at its thickest point?
53964.e: At its thickest point the ice is more than 3000 metres thick. Under this weight, the bedrock in the middle of the island has been pressed down.
53964.m: The Greenland ice sheet is over 3 kilometres thick.

53965.q: By how much would sea level rise if the whole Greenland ice sheet melted?
53965.e: Greenland's ice holds enough water to raise sea level by about 7 metres. However, melting completely would take centuries to thousands of years.
53965.m: All of Greenland's ice would raise the oceans by about 7 metres.

53966.q: Which mass of ice is even bigger than the Greenland ice sheet?
53966.e: The Greenland ice sheet is the second-largest mass of ice on Earth. Only the Antarctic ice sheet is bigger.
53966.m: Only Antarctica's ice is bigger than Greenland's.

53967.q: Why is the Ilulissat Icefjord in Greenland a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: A very fast glacier produces huge icebergs there
The oldest houses in the world stand there
There is a tropical beach there
53967.e: The glacier Sermeq Kujalleq flows into the Ilulissat Icefjord. It is one of the fastest glaciers in the world and produces a great many icebergs.
53967.m: The Ilulissat Icefjord is a World Heritage Site full of icebergs.

53968.q: What did the Swiss scientist Alfred de Quervain achieve in Greenland in 1912?
a: He crossed the ice sheet from west to east
He was the first to climb Mount Everest
He was the first to reach the South Pole
53968.e: In 1912 Alfred de Quervain and his team crossed the Greenland ice sheet. It was one of the first crossings of Greenland.
53968.m: Alfred de Quervain crossed the Greenland ice in 1912.

53969.q: Why do researchers drill deep ice cores from the Greenland ice sheet?
a: to study the climate of the past
53969.e: Tiny air bubbles and dust from many thousands of years are trapped in the ice. From them you can read the climate of the past; the University of Bern also researches this.
53969.m: Ice cores reveal what the climate used to be like.

53970.e: In their language, Inuit means “people”. A single person is called an Inuk.

53971.q: Why do the Inuit put figures made of piled-up stones in the landscape?
53971.e: Such a stone figure is called an inuksuk, plural inuksuit. They show things like routes, hunting grounds or food stores.
53971.m: Inuit stone figures show the way.

53972.q: What is the language of the Inuit in eastern Canada called?
53972.e: Inuktitut is an official language in Nunavut. It is written with its own syllabic script or with Latin letters.
53972.m: Many Inuit in Canada speak Inuktitut.

53973.q: What did Inuit women use the ulu, a knife with a crescent-shaped blade, for?
a: For cutting up meat and cutting furs
For digging holes in the ice
53973.e: The ulu has a curved blade and a handle in the middle. It is used for cutting up meat and fish and for cutting furs to shape.
53973.m: The ulu is the traditional knife of Inuit women.

53974.q: From where did the ancestors of the Inuit spread as far as Greenland about 1000 years ago?
53974.e: The people of the Thule culture moved east from Alaska all the way to Greenland. They are considered the direct ancestors of today's Inuit.
53974.m: The ancestors of the Inuit came from Alaska.

53975.q: Which older name given to the Inuit by outsiders do many Inuit reject today, especially in Canada and Greenland?
53975.e: The name “Eskimo” does not come from the Inuit themselves. In Canada and Greenland it has mostly been replaced by “Inuit” today.
53975.m: In Canada and Greenland people say Inuit instead of Eskimo.

53976.q: How does the traditional throat singing of Inuit women work?
a: Two women sing facing each other, and whoever laughs first loses
One woman sings alone on a mountain
Many women sing as a choir in church
The women only sing under water
53976.e: In katajjaq, two singers stand facing each other and take turns making rhythmic sounds. Whoever has to laugh first or loses the rhythm loses.
53976.m: In Inuit throat singing, whoever laughs first loses.

53977.q: What were the traditional Inuit snow goggles with narrow slits used for?
53977.e: The goggles, made of bone, wood or ivory, let only a little light through the slits. This protects the eyes from the glaring sunlight reflected by the snow.
53977.m: Snow goggles protected the Inuit from snow blindness.

53978.q: Roughly during which period can you see the midnight sun at the North Cape?
a: from mid-May to the end of July
53978.e: The North Cape lies far north of the Arctic Circle. There the sun stays above the horizon around the clock from about mid-May to the end of July.
53978.m: At the North Cape the midnight sun shines from May to July.

53979.q: On which day can the midnight sun be seen exactly at the Arctic Circle?
53979.e: At the Arctic Circle the sun stays up all night only once, at the summer solstice. The further north you travel, the longer the period of midnight sun lasts.
53979.m: At the Arctic Circle the midnight sun only appears at the summer solstice.

53980.q: How does the sun move across the sky at the North Pole during the polar day?
a: It circles all the way round the horizon.
It climbs until it is straight overhead.
It stands still at one point.
It rises and sets every hour.
53980.e: At the pole the sun stays at roughly the same height all day. It travels once around the whole horizon each day.
53980.m: At the pole the summer sun circles the horizon.

53981.q: Which country is often called the “Land of the Midnight Sun”?
53981.e: A large part of Norway lies north of the Arctic Circle. That is why the country uses the nickname “Land of the Midnight Sun”.
53981.m: Norway is called the Land of the Midnight Sun.

53982.q: Who was the first to sail all the way through the Northwest Passage?
53982.e: Roald Amundsen sailed through the passage in the small ship Gjøa from 1903 to 1906. He spent several winters stuck in the ice.
53982.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to conquer the Northwest Passage.

53983.q: Which group of islands does the Northwest Passage pass through?
53983.e: There are several possible routes between the many islands in northern Canada. They are often blocked by ice.
53983.m: The Northwest Passage runs through the islands of northern Canada.

53984.q: What is the sea route along the northern coast of Russia from the Atlantic to the Pacific called?
53984.e: The Northeast Passage is the counterpart of the Northwest Passage. It runs along Siberia through the Arctic Ocean.
53984.m: The Northeast Passage runs along the coast of Russia.

53985.q: Why can ships use the Northwest Passage in summer more often today than in the past?
a: because the Arctic sea ice is shrinking
because the current has become stronger
53985.e: Because of global warming, more sea ice melts in summer. For some years now the passage has therefore had little ice at times.
53985.m: Less sea ice makes the Northwest Passage easier to sail through.

53986.q: Why were European traders interested in the Northwest Passage from early on?
a: as a shorter sea route to Asia
as a route to gold mines in Africa
53986.e: For centuries, sailors searched for a northern route to China and India. It was meant to save them the long voyage around South America or Africa.
53986.m: The Northwest Passage was meant to be a short route to Asia.

53987.q: Which sailor, searching for the Northwest Passage in 1610, discovered a large bay that is named after him today?
53987.e: In 1610 Henry Hudson reached the huge bay in Canada. After a mutiny he was set adrift there and was never seen again.
53987.m: Henry Hudson gave his name to Hudson Bay.

53988.q: Which country regards the waters of the Northwest Passage as its own internal waters?
53988.e: Canada sees the passage as part of its own territory. Other countries, such as the USA, regard it as an international strait.
53988.m: Canada claims the Northwest Passage as its own waters.

53989.q: What happens when wind and currents push ice floes against each other?
a: They break and pile up into ridges
53989.e: The floes break at their edges and push over one another. This creates ice ridges that can be several metres high.
53989.m: Ice that is pushed together piles up into ridges.

53990.q: Why are open patches of water in the middle of the pack ice so important for seals?
a: They can come up there to breathe
It is warmer there than on land
53990.e: Seals are mammals and need air. In open patches in the ice they can surface and breathe.
53990.m: Seals need holes in the ice to breathe.

53991.q: What have satellite images shown for decades about Arctic sea ice in summer?
a: There is less and less of it
There is more and more of it
53991.e: Satellites have been observing the sea ice since the late 1970s. The area of ice in summer has become much smaller since then.
53991.m: Arctic summer sea ice is shrinking.

53992.q: What do you call sea ice that has survived at least one summer?
53992.e: Multi-year ice is thicker and firmer than ice that only formed last winter. There is much less of it in the Arctic today than in the past.
53992.m: Ice that survives a summer is called multi-year ice.

53993.q: At roughly what latitude does the Arctic Circle lie?
53993.e: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66.5 degrees north. This comes from 90 degrees minus the tilt of the Earth's axis of about 23.5 degrees.
53993.m: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66.5 degrees north.

53994.q: Which of these countries is NOT crossed by the Arctic Circle?
53994.e: Estonia lies at about 58 to 60 degrees north, well south of the Arctic Circle. Finland, Sweden and Norway all reach beyond the Arctic Circle.
53994.m: Estonia lies entirely south of the Arctic Circle.

53995.q: Which Finnish town is known for lying right on the Arctic Circle?
53995.e: Rovaniemi is the capital of Lapland. A few kilometres north of the centre runs the Arctic Circle, where there is also a well-known Santa Claus village.
53995.m: Rovaniemi lies in Lapland on the Arctic Circle.

53996.q: Why is it almost light in Iceland in June, even at midnight?
a: Because Iceland lies very close to the Arctic Circle
Because Iceland lies on the equator
Because the moon shines brighter there
53996.e: Iceland lies just south of the Arctic Circle. In summer the sun sets there only briefly, and it never gets properly dark.
53996.m: Near the Arctic Circle, summer nights are light.

53998.q: What is true for every place north of the Arctic Circle?
a: There is at least one day without a sunset.
There is snow all year round.
The sun is directly overhead at noon.
53998.e: North of the Arctic Circle the sun stays above the horizon all day at least once in summer. That is exactly how the Arctic Circle is defined.
53998.m: North of the Arctic Circle there are days without a sunset.

53999.q: Which continent lies almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle?
53999.e: The Antarctic Circle lies at about 66.5 degrees south. Only a narrow part of the continent reaches north beyond it.
53999.m: Antarctica lies almost entirely inside the Antarctic Circle.

54000.q: What causes the polar night and the polar day?
a: the tilt of the Earth's axis
54000.e: The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees. So in winter one pole faces away from the sun while the other is lit all the time.
54000.m: Polar night and polar day are caused by the tilted axis of the Earth.

54001.q: Around which date is the polar night in the Arctic at its longest?
54001.e: At the winter solstice the North Pole is tilted furthest away from the sun. That is when the polar night reaches its greatest extent.
54001.m: In the north, the polar night is greatest at the winter solstice.

54002.q: Why is it not completely dark at noon during the polar night near the Arctic Circle?
a: The sun is just below the horizon and creates twilight.
The moon shines brightly every day.
54002.e: At the Arctic Circle the sun is only slightly below the horizon during the polar night. Its light is scattered in the air, so there is twilight around midday.
54002.m: During the polar night there is often twilight at noon.

54003.q: How does the length of the polar night change the closer you get to the pole?
54003.e: At the Arctic Circle the polar night lasts only about one day in theory. The further you travel towards the pole, the more days the sun stays below the horizon.
54003.m: The closer to the pole, the longer the polar night.

54004.q: Which country is the Ross Ice Shelf roughly the same size as?
54004.e: At about 480,000 square kilometres, the Ross Ice Shelf is the largest ice shelf on Earth and about the size of France. Switzerland would fit into it more than ten times.
54004.m: The Ross Ice Shelf is about the size of France.

54005.q: On which continent are the largest ice shelves on Earth?
54005.e: The two largest ice shelves, the Ross and the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf, lie on the edge of Antarctica. Each is almost as big as France.
54005.m: The largest ice shelves are in Antarctica.

54006.q: What happened to a large ice shelf in Antarctica in 2002?
a: It broke apart within a few weeks
It was towed away by ships
54006.e: In February and March 2002 the Larsen B Ice Shelf broke into thousands of pieces. Scientists see the strong warming in this region as an important cause.
54006.m: In 2002 a large ice shelf in Antarctica fell apart.

54007.q: What important job does an ice shelf do for the glaciers behind it?
a: It slows their flow into the sea.
It keeps snow away from them.
54007.e: An ice shelf acts like a plug in front of the glaciers. If it disappears, the glaciers often flow faster into the sea, which makes sea levels rise.
54007.m: An ice shelf holds back the glaciers like a cork.

54008.q: Where does an ice shelf mainly melt?
a: only on the surface, from the sun
54008.e: Seawater that is warmer than the ice flows beneath the ice shelf. So a large part of the ice shelf melts from below.
54008.m: Ice shelves melt mainly from below.

54010.q: What do you call a large piece of ice that breaks off an ice shelf and drifts in the sea?
54010.e: Pieces keep breaking off at the edge of the ice shelf. They drift through the sea as icebergs, sometimes enormous ones.
54010.m: Broken-off pieces of ice shelf drift in the sea as icebergs.

54011.q: Which country does Svalbard belong to?
54011.e: Under the Svalbard Treaty, the archipelago, whose main island is Spitsbergen, is under Norwegian sovereignty. However, citizens of the treaty countries may do business there.

54012.q: What do people on Svalbard experience in summer?
a: The sun does not set for weeks
It rains every day like in a rainforest
The sun never rises at all
54012.e: Svalbard lies far north of the Arctic Circle. In summer the midnight sun shines, in winter there is polar night.
54012.m: On Svalbard the midnight sun shines in summer.

54013.q: What is stored in the Global Seed Vault on Svalbard?
54013.e: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault lies inside a mountain near Longyearbyen. Seed samples from all over the world are kept there as a reserve in case of disasters.
54013.m: The vault on Svalbard keeps plant seeds safe for the future.

54014.q: In which sea does Svalbard lie?
54014.e: Svalbard lies between Norway and the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean. Many glaciers cover the islands.
54014.m: Svalbard lies in the Arctic Ocean.

54015.q: Where does the island of Spitsbergen get its name from?
a: from the pointed teeth of walruses
54015.e: The Dutch sailor Willem Barentsz saw the pointed peaks of the islands in 1596. So he named them Spitsbergen, meaning “pointed mountains”.
54015.m: Spitsbergen is named after its pointed mountains.

54016.q: How long does it stay dark on Svalbard in winter?
54016.e: Because Svalbard lies so far north, the sun does not rise for months in winter. This time is called the polar night.
54016.m: On Svalbard the polar night lasts several months.

54017.q: Why must people on Svalbard carry protection against animals outside the settlements?
54017.e: Polar bears live on Svalbard and can be dangerous to people. Outside the settlements, suitable protection is therefore strongly required.
54017.m: On Svalbard you have to protect yourself from polar bears.

54018.q: Which is the smallest of the five oceans?
54018.e: The Arctic Ocean around the North Pole is the smallest ocean. It is also the shallowest on average.
54018.m: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest ocean.

54019.q: Roughly what percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by sea?
54019.e: About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is sea. That is why the Earth is also called the “Blue Planet”.
54019.m: About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered by sea.

54020.q: Which ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia?
54020.e: The Indian Ocean is the third largest ocean. It is bordered by Africa to the west, Asia to the north and Australia to the east.
54020.m: The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia.

54021.q: Who gave the Pacific its name, which means “peaceful”?
54021.e: On his voyage around the world in 1520, Magellan had calm weather on the new ocean. So he called it “Mar Pacífico”, the peaceful sea.
54021.m: Magellan named the Pacific the peaceful sea.

54022.q: In which month is the sea ice in the Arctic Ocean usually at its smallest?
54022.e: At the end of the Arctic summer, the most ice has melted. So the minimum is usually reached in September and the maximum in March.
