54022.m: Arctic sea ice is smallest in September.

54023.q: Which large predator hunts seals on the Arctic sea ice?
54023.e: Polar bears live on the sea ice and hunt seals there. Penguins, on the other hand, live almost only in the Southern Hemisphere.
54023.m: The polar bear needs the sea ice to hunt.

54024.q: What is the sea route north of Canada between the Atlantic and the Pacific called?
54024.e: The Northwest Passage runs through the islands of northern Canada. Roald Amundsen was the first to sail all the way through it, from 1903 to 1906.
54024.m: The Northwest Passage runs past the north of Canada.

54025.q: Why did Fridtjof Nansen deliberately let his ship freeze into the Arctic pack ice in 1893?
a: To drift across the Arctic with the ice
To save fuel for the winter
To build a town on the ice
54025.e: Nansen wanted to prove that the sea ice drifts across the Arctic. His ship, the Fram, drifted with the ice for three years.
54025.m: Nansen drifted across the Arctic with his ship in the ice.

54026.q: Which continent does the Southern Ocean surround?
54026.e: The Southern Ocean completely surrounds Antarctica. It is also called the Antarctic Ocean.
54026.m: The Southern Ocean flows all the way round Antarctica.

54027.q: What is another name for the Southern Ocean?
54027.e: The Southern Ocean lies around Antarctica, that is, around the South Pole. That is why it is also called the Antarctic Ocean.
54027.m: The Southern Ocean is also called the Antarctic Ocean.

54028.q: What is the strong current that flows all the way round Antarctica called?
54028.e: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows from west to east around Antarctica. It carries more water than any other ocean current.
54028.m: The Circumpolar Current circles Antarctica without any obstacle.

54029.q: Which strait lies between the southern tip of South America and Antarctica?
54029.e: The Drake Passage is notorious for high waves and storms. It is the narrowest part of the Southern Ocean.
54029.m: The Drake Passage separates South America from Antarctica.

54030.q: Which birds that cannot fly live on the coasts of the Southern Ocean?
54030.e: Penguins are flightless seabirds of the Southern Hemisphere. The emperor penguin even breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter.
54030.m: Penguins swim well but cannot fly.

54031.q: How many oceans do many maps show today if you count the Southern Ocean?
54031.e: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern Oceans make five oceans. Since 2021 the National Geographic Society has also shown the Southern Ocean on its maps.
54031.m: Since 2021 many maps show five oceans.

54032.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point of the Mariana Trench?
54032.e: The deepest point lies almost 11,000 metres below sea level. Mount Everest would fit inside and still be more than 2 kilometres under water.
54032.m: The Mariana Trench is almost 11 kilometres deep.

54033.q: Which Swiss man dived to the bottom of the Mariana Trench with Don Walsh in the submersible “Trieste” in 1960?
54033.e: In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first people to reach the deepest point of the sea. The submersible had been designed by his father, Auguste Piccard.
54033.m: In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point on Earth.

54034.q: What is the deepest point in the Mariana Trench called?
54034.e: The deepest point is called the Challenger Deep. It is named after the British research ship Challenger.
54034.m: The Challenger Deep is the deepest point in the sea.

54035.q: How did the Mariana Trench form?
a: One tectonic plate is pushing under another.
54035.e: Here the Pacific Plate sinks beneath the Philippine Plate. This creates a long, very deep trench.
54035.m: Deep-sea trenches form where one plate sinks under another.

54036.q: Which film director dived alone in a submersible to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 2012?
54036.e: In 2012 James Cameron reached the deepest point of the trench in the submersible “Deepsea Challenger”. He was the first person to dive there alone.
54036.m: In 2012 James Cameron dived alone into the Mariana Trench.

54037.q: What is especially extreme at the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
54037.e: At a depth of almost 11 kilometres the pressure is more than a thousand times greater than at the surface. Only specially built submersibles can withstand it.
54037.m: The deeper you dive, the greater the water pressure.

a: a mountain range under the sea
54038.e: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a huge mountain range on the seabed. It runs from north to south through the whole Atlantic.
54038.m: An underwater mountain range runs down the middle of the Atlantic.

54039.q: What happens to the tectonic plates at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
a: They move away from each other.
They crash head-on into each other.
One plate sinks under the other.
They do not move at all.
54039.e: At the ridge the plates drift apart. Magma rises from the gap and forms new seabed.
54039.m: The seabed grows at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

54040.q: Roughly how much wider does the Atlantic get each year at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
54040.e: The plates move apart by only about 2 to 5 centimetres a year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
54040.m: The Atlantic gets a few centimetres wider every year.

54041.q: Which Portuguese group of islands lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
54041.e: The Azores lie in the middle of the Atlantic on the ridge. They are volcanic in origin.
54041.m: The Azores are volcanic islands on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

54042.q: Where is the seabed in the Atlantic youngest?
a: on the coasts of the Americas
54042.e: New seabed is constantly forming at the ridge. The further you go from the ridge, the older the rock is.
54042.m: The youngest seabed lies at the mid-ocean ridge.

54043.q: What did scientists discover in the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
54043.e: In the 1950s the scientist Marie Tharp drew maps of the seabed. In doing so she discovered a rift valley where the tectonic plates drift apart.
54043.m: A rift valley lies in the middle of the ridge.

54044.q: Where does the warm Gulf Stream come from?
54044.e: The Gulf Stream is named after the Gulf of Mexico. It flows north along the east coast of North America.
54044.m: The Gulf Stream comes from the Gulf of Mexico.

54045.q: What effect do the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current have on north-west Europe?
54045.e: The warm water gives off heat to the air. Westerly winds carry this heat to Europe, which is therefore milder than other areas at the same latitude.
54045.m: The Gulf Stream is Europe's central heating.

54046.q: What is the continuation of the Gulf Stream towards Europe called?
54046.e: East of Newfoundland the Gulf Stream becomes the North Atlantic Current. This brings warm water as far as Norway.
54046.m: The North Atlantic Current continues the Gulf Stream.

54047.q: Which American statesman had one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream printed around 1770?
54047.e: Benjamin Franklin was postmaster and wanted to speed up the post to Europe. Together with a ship's captain, he had the Gulf Stream drawn on a map.
54047.m: Benjamin Franklin made the Gulf Stream well known.

54048.q: Why do harbours in northern Norway usually stay free of ice even in winter?
a: because of the warm North Atlantic Current
because there is no winter there
because of the high salt content of the fjords
54048.e: The North Atlantic Current, the continuation of the Gulf Stream, brings warm water far to the north. That is why harbours such as Hammerfest do not freeze over.
54048.m: Thanks to warm Atlantic water, Norway's harbours stay ice-free.

54049.q: What did the Spanish explorer Ponce de León notice off Florida in 1513?
a: His ships drifted backwards despite the wind
54049.e: A strong ocean current pushed Ponce de León's ships back. It was the current that was later called the Gulf Stream.
54049.m: Ponce de León noticed the Gulf Stream as early as 1513.

54050.q: What does the great current system in the Atlantic, which the Gulf Stream is part of, carry?
a: Warm water northwards, cold deep water southwards
Ice from the North Pole to the equator
Sand from the Sahara to America
54050.e: The Gulf Stream is part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. At the surface warm water flows north, and deep down cold water flows south.
54050.m: The Gulf Stream is part of the great overturning circulation in the Atlantic.

54051.q: Which two things mainly drive ocean currents?
a: Wind and differences in temperature and salt content
54051.e: Surface currents are driven mainly by the wind. Deep currents form because cold, salty water is heavier and sinks.
54051.m: Wind, temperature and salt move the seawater.

54052.q: Which cold current flows off the coast of Peru and Chile?
54052.e: The Humboldt Current carries cold, nutrient-rich water northwards. It is named after the explorer Alexander von Humboldt.
54052.m: The Humboldt Current cools the coast of South America.

54053.q: What is the weather event called in which the water off Peru warms up strongly?
54053.e: During El Niño the trade winds weaken and warm water spreads off South America. This changes the weather around the world.
54053.m: El Niño warms the Pacific off South America.

54054.q: Where do most icebergs in the North Atlantic come from, like the one the Titanic hit in 1912?
54054.e: On the coast of Greenland, icebergs break off the glaciers. Cold currents carry them south into the shipping lanes.
54054.m: Icebergs in the North Atlantic mostly come from Greenland.

54055.q: Which warm ocean current gives western Europe a mild climate?
54055.e: The Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Caribbean across the Atlantic to Europe. That is why winters in Norway, for example, are milder than in Canada at the same latitude.
54055.m: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe.

54056.q: Which desert on the coast of Africa is especially dry because of the cold Benguela Current?
54056.e: The cold water cools the air and prevents rain. That is why the Namib coastal desert in Namibia is extremely dry.
54056.m: Cold ocean currents help create coastal deserts.

54057.q: What is another name for the worldwide system of surface and deep currents?
54057.e: Warm water flows at the surface, cools, sinks and flows back in the depths. This worldwide system is called the global conveyor belt.
54057.m: The global conveyor belt links all the oceans.

54058.q: Where does especially large amounts of plastic rubbish collect in the North Pacific?
a: at the mouth of the Amazon
54058.e: Ocean currents form huge gyres, and floating rubbish collects in their centre. The largest known garbage patch lies between Hawaii and California.
54058.m: Ocean gyres collect plastic rubbish in their centre.

54059.q: Roughly how many times a day is there high tide on the North Sea coast?
54059.e: There are about 12 hours and 25 minutes between two high tides. So there are usually two high tides and two low tides each day.
54059.m: Low tide and high tide alternate about every six hours.

54060.q: What is a particularly high tide at full or new moon called?
54060.e: At full and new moon the sun, moon and Earth are in a line. Their forces add together, and the difference between low and high tide is especially large.
54060.m: At full and new moon there is a spring tide.

54061.q: What do you call the difference in height between low and high tide?
54061.e: The tidal range is the difference between low water and high water. It varies greatly from coast to coast.
54061.m: The tidal range measures the difference between low and high tide.

54062.q: Where is the largest tidal range in the world?
54062.e: In the Bay of Fundy the difference between low and high tide can be about 16 metres. The shape of the bay strengthens the tides.
54062.m: The Bay of Fundy has the largest tidal range.

54063.q: Why are the tides only weak in the Mediterranean?
a: because it is almost completely surrounded by land
because there is no moon there
because the water is too warm
54063.e: The Mediterranean is connected to the Atlantic only by the narrow Strait of Gibraltar. So the tidal range is usually only a few tens of centimetres.
54063.m: In the Mediterranean you hardly notice the tides.

54064.q: Where does a tidal power station like the one on the Rance in France get its electricity from?
54064.e: The Rance tidal power station in Brittany has used the flow of the tides since 1966. Turbines in the dam turn as seawater flows in and out.
54064.m: Tidal power stations make electricity from the tides.

54065.q: Roughly how much salt does a litre of seawater contain on average?
54065.e: Seawater has an average salt content of about 3.5 per cent. That is about 35 grams of salt per litre.
54065.m: A litre of seawater contains about 35 grams of salt.

54066.q: Which salt makes up most of sea salt?
54066.e: In chemistry, table salt is called sodium chloride. It makes up most of the salts dissolved in the sea.
54066.m: Sea salt consists mainly of table salt.

54067.q: Where does a large part of the salt in the sea come from?
a: from rock washed out by rivers
54067.e: Rain and rivers dissolve minerals from rock and carry them to the sea. The water evaporates, but the salt stays behind and builds up.
54067.m: Rivers bring dissolved salts from rock into the sea.

54068.q: What do you call a mixture of fresh water and salt water, like in the Baltic Sea?
54068.e: The Baltic Sea receives a lot of fresh water from rivers and only a little salt water from the North Sea. So its water is brackish, with little salt.
54068.m: Brackish water is a mixture of fresh water and salt water.

54069.q: Which marginal sea has a particularly high salt content of about 4 per cent?
54069.e: In the Red Sea a lot of water evaporates because of the heat, and hardly any rivers flow into it. That is why it is saltier than average.
54069.m: Heat and little inflow make the Red Sea very salty.

54070.q: What is getting drinking water from seawater called?
54070.e: In desalination the salt is removed from the water. Dry countries by the sea in particular use this technique.
54070.m: Desalination plants turn seawater into drinking water.

54071.q: Why is it easier to swim in the salty sea than in a Swiss lake?
a: Salt water has a higher density.
There are waves in the sea.
54071.e: Salt water is heavier than the same amount of fresh water. So the body gets more buoyancy in the sea.
54071.m: You float more easily in salt water than in fresh water.

54072.q: Which sea does the water of the Inn from the Engadine flow into?
54072.e: The Inn flows into the Danube at Passau. The Danube flows all the way to the Black Sea.
54072.m: Water from the Inn reaches the Black Sea via the Danube.

54073.q: Which strait connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara?
54073.e: The Bosporus runs right through the city of Istanbul. It separates Europe from Asia.
54073.m: The Bosporus links the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara.

54074.q: What is a sea called that is separated from the open ocean only by islands or peninsulas, like the North Sea?
54074.e: A marginal sea lies on the edge of an ocean and is broadly connected to it. The North Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic.
54074.m: The North Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic.

54075.q: Via which river does water from Ticino reach the Adriatic Sea?
54075.e: The river Ticino flows through Lake Maggiore and into the Po. The Po reaches the Adriatic Sea south of Venice.
54075.m: Water from Ticino flows via the Po into the Adriatic.

54076.q: Which canal has linked the Caribbean Sea with the Pacific since 1914?
54076.e: The Panama Canal runs through the narrow Isthmus of Panama. It saves ships the long voyage around South America.
54076.m: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and the Pacific.

54077.q: Which weather events threaten the Caribbean mainly from June to November?
54077.e: Tropical storms form over the warm water of the Atlantic. In the Caribbean and the North Atlantic they are called hurricanes.
54077.m: In the Caribbean tropical storms are called hurricanes.

54078.q: Which ocean does the South China Sea belong to?
54078.e: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the western Pacific. It lies between southern China, Vietnam, the Philippines and Borneo.
54078.m: The South China Sea belongs to the Pacific.

54079.q: Which strait connects the South China Sea with the Indian Ocean?
54079.e: The Strait of Malacca lies between Malaysia and the island of Sumatra. It is one of the busiest shipping routes in the world.
54079.m: Huge numbers of cargo ships pass through the Strait of Malacca.

54080.q: Which group of islands in the South China Sea is claimed by several countries?
54080.e: Several neighbouring countries claim the Spratly Islands, including China, Vietnam and the Philippines. The area is important for fishing and raw materials.
54080.m: Several countries are in dispute over the Spratly Islands.

54081.q: Which city lies at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula near the South China Sea?
54081.e: Singapore lies where the Strait of Malacca meets the South China Sea. Its port is one of the largest in the world.
54081.m: Singapore lies on one of the most important sea routes in the world.

54082.q: Which country does NOT border the South China Sea?
54082.e: Vietnam, the Philippines and Malaysia lie on the South China Sea. Japan lies further north, on the East China Sea and the Pacific.
54082.m: Many countries of South-East Asia lie on the South China Sea.

54083.q: What do you call a coral reef that grows right on the coast, with no lagoon in between?
54083.e: A fringing reef grows directly along the shore of a coast or island. With a barrier reef, by contrast, there is a lagoon between the reef and the land.
54083.m: A fringing reef grows right on the coast.

54084.q: Which gas does the sea absorb from the air, making the water more acidic so that corals find it harder to build their limestone?
54084.e: When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, carbonic acid forms and the water becomes more acidic. This ocean acidification makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeletons.
54084.m: More carbon dioxide makes the sea more acidic and harms the corals.

54085.q: What conditions do reef-building corals need?
54085.e: The algae inside the corals need sunlight. That is why reefs grow in warm, clear seawater that is not too deep.
54085.m: Coral reefs need light and warmth.

54086.q: What material do corals build their skeleton from?
54086.e: Coral polyps form a skeleton of limestone. Over thousands of years these skeletons grow into huge reefs.
54086.m: Reefs are made of the limestone of countless corals.

54087.q: Roughly what share of the sea's area do coral reefs cover?
54087.e: Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the seabed. Yet about a quarter of all marine species live there.
54087.m: Coral reefs are small but full of life.

54088.q: What is it called when deep-sea animals produce their own light?
54088.e: In the deep sea it is completely dark. Many animals produce their own light to lure prey or to find a partner.
54088.m: Many deep-sea animals make their own light.

54089.q: What are hot springs on the seabed, from which dark, mineral-rich water pours, called?
54089.e: Black smokers are hydrothermal vents in the deep sea. Around them live animals that do not depend on sunlight.
54089.m: Around black smokers there is life without sunlight.

54090.q: How cold is the water in the deep sea usually?
54090.e: Cold water is heavy and sinks to the depths. That is why it is only a few degrees warm almost everywhere at the bottom of the oceans.
54090.m: The deep sea is dark and cold.

54091.q: By roughly how much does water pressure increase for every 10 metres of depth?
54091.e: Every 10 metres of depth adds about 1 bar of pressure. So at a depth of 4000 metres it is about 400 bar.
54091.m: Every ten metres the pressure rises by about one bar.

54092.q: Which lumpy raw materials lie on some deep-sea floors?
54092.e: Manganese nodules contain metals such as manganese, nickel and copper. They grow extremely slowly over millions of years.
54092.m: Metal-rich manganese nodules lie on the deep-sea floor.

54093.q: Roughly how deep are the oceans on average?
54093.e: The average depth of all the oceans is about 3700 metres. So most of the seabed belongs to the deep sea.
54093.m: Most of the sea is deep sea.

54094.q: Which is the warmest ocean on Earth?
54094.e: Most of the Indian Ocean lies in the tropics. In the north it does not reach into cold regions, so it is the warmest ocean.
54094.m: The Indian Ocean is the warmest ocean.

54095.q: What do you call all the connected oceans and seas together?
54095.e: All the oceans are connected and form one single huge body of water. This is called the world ocean.
54095.m: Together, all the oceans form the world ocean.

54097.q: On which island does the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rise out of the sea, so that you can see the gap between two tectonic plates on land?
54097.e: Iceland lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. In Thingvellir National Park you can see the North American and Eurasian plates drifting apart.
54097.m: In Iceland you can see the Mid-Atlantic Ridge on land.

54098.q: What is the weak tide at half moon called?
54098.e: At half moon the sun and moon are at right angles to the Earth. Their forces partly cancel out, and the tidal range is small.
54098.m: At half moon the tide is weak.

54099.q: Which French mount with an abbey is often completely surrounded by the sea at high tide?
54099.e: Mont-Saint-Michel lies in a bay with a very large tidal range. At high tide it becomes an island, at low tide it stands on the mudflats.
54099.m: Mont-Saint-Michel becomes an island at high tide.

54100.q: What are the sites called where sea salt is obtained by evaporating seawater?
54100.e: In shallow basins on the coast the water evaporates in the sun. What is left is the salt, which is harvested.
54100.m: In salt pans the salt is left behind after evaporation.

54101.q: Which sea lies between Greece and Turkey?
54101.e: The Aegean Sea is part of the Mediterranean. It is known for its many islands, such as Crete and the Cyclades.
54101.m: The Aegean lies between Greece and Turkey.

54102.q: What is the group of islands made up of Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico called?
54102.e: The Greater Antilles are the largest islands on the northern edge of the Caribbean Sea. The many smaller islands to the east are called the Lesser Antilles.
54102.m: Cuba and Jamaica belong to the Greater Antilles.

54103.q: Which South American country with the capital Caracas lies on the Caribbean Sea?
54103.e: Venezuela has a long coast on the Caribbean Sea. Peru and Chile lie on the Pacific, and Paraguay has no coast at all.

54104.q: Off which Central American country is there a large barrier reef in the Caribbean?
54104.e: The Belize Barrier Reef is part of the Mesoamerican Reef. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
54104.m: A large coral reef in the Caribbean lies off Belize.

54105.q: Which large city with special status in China lies on the South China Sea?
54105.e: Hong Kong lies where the Pearl River flows into the South China Sea. It is a special administrative region of China with a large port.
54105.m: Hong Kong lies on the South China Sea.

54107.q: Which colourful fish lives protected among the tentacles of sea anemones on the reef?
54107.e: The clownfish has a layer of slime that protects it from the anemone's stinging poison. The anemone protects it from enemies.
54107.m: The clownfish lives in the sea anemone.

54108.q: Which naturalist explained in the 19th century how ring-shaped reefs form around sinking islands?
54108.e: Darwin saw many reefs on his voyage on the Beagle. He realised that corals grow upwards while a volcanic island slowly sinks.
54108.m: Darwin explained how ring reefs form.

54109.q: Below roughly what depth is the sea practically completely dark?
54109.e: Sunlight is gradually swallowed by the water. Below about 1000 metres no measurable sunlight arrives any more.
54109.m: Below a thousand metres the sea is in endless night.

54110.q: Why do no plants grow in the deep sea?
a: because the water is too salty
because it is too warm there
54110.e: Plants need light for photosynthesis. So they cannot grow in the dark deep sea.
54110.m: Without light no plants can grow.

54111.q: Which Norwegian group of islands lies in the Arctic Ocean?
54111.e: Svalbard lies far north of the Norwegian mainland. Much of the islands is covered by glaciers.
54111.m: Svalbard lies in the middle of the Arctic.

54112.q: Which ocean borders the west coast of North and South America?
54112.e: West of the Americas, the Pacific stretches as far as Asia and Australia. The east coast of the Americas, by contrast, lies on the Atlantic.
54112.m: The west coast of the Americas lies on the Pacific.

54113.q: Which seabird, with the largest wingspan of any bird, glides over the Southern Ocean?
54113.e: The wandering albatross can reach a wingspan of more than 3 metres. It glides over the sea for days, hardly flapping its wings.
54113.m: The wandering albatross has the largest wings of any bird.

54114.q: Which sea lies between mainland Italy and the islands of Corsica and Sardinia?
54114.e: The Tyrrhenian Sea is part of the Mediterranean. In the south it is bordered by Sicily.
54114.m: The Tyrrhenian Sea lies west of Italy.

54115.q: Which European kingdom does the Caribbean island of Curaçao belong to?
54115.e: Like Aruba and Bonaire, Curaçao is one of the ABC islands off the coast of Venezuela. The islands are part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
54115.m: Curaçao belongs to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

54116.q: Which whale with a long, twisted tusk lives in the Arctic Ocean?
54116.e: In male narwhals, one tooth usually grows into a tusk 2 to 3 metres long. The narwhal lives in Arctic waters all year round.
54116.m: The narwhal is the unicorn of the Arctic.

54117.q: Which river is the second longest in Europe after the Volga?
54117.e: The Danube is about 2850 km long and flows into the Black Sea. Only the Volga is longer in Europe.
54117.m: The Danube is the second longest river in Europe.

54118.q: Which river system, at about 6000 km, is the longest in North America?
54118.e: If you measure the Mississippi together with its long tributary, the Missouri, you get about 6000 km. The system flows into the Gulf of Mexico.
54118.m: Together, the Mississippi and Missouri form the longest river system in North America.

54119.q: Which river is the longest in France?
54119.e: The Loire is about 1000 km long and flows entirely within France. It reaches the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire.
54119.m: The Loire is the longest river in France.

54120.q: Which ocean do the great Siberian rivers Ob, Yenisei and Lena flow into?
54120.e: The three rivers flow from south to north through Siberia. They flow into the Arctic Ocean.
54120.m: The great rivers of Siberia flow north into the Arctic Ocean.

54121.q: Roughly how long is the Yangtze, the longest river in Asia?
54121.e: The Yangtze is about 6300 km long, making it the third longest river on Earth after the Nile and the Amazon. It flows only through China.
54121.m: The Yangtze is about 6300 kilometres long.

54122.q: Which river is the longest in Canada?
54122.e: The Mackenzie flows about 1700 km north from Great Slave Lake to the Arctic Ocean. With its headwaters, the river system is more than 4000 km long.
54122.m: The Mackenzie is the longest river in Canada.

54123.q: Roughly how much water does the Amazon carry per second at its mouth on average?
54123.e: The Amazon's average flow is more than 200,000 cubic metres per second. The Rhine at Basel carries on average only about 1000 cubic metres per second.
54123.m: The Amazon carries about 200,000 cubic metres of water into the sea every second.

54124.q: Roughly what share of all the river water that flows into the seas comes from the Amazon?
54124.e: About 20 per cent of the fresh water that all the rivers together bring to the oceans comes from the Amazon. This is due to the huge amounts of rain in the tropical rainforest.
54124.m: About a fifth of all the river water on Earth comes from the Amazon.

54125.q: What is the high tidal wave called that runs up the Amazon from the sea at spring tide?
54125.e: The pororoca is a tidal bore that can be several metres high and travel far upstream. Surfers sometimes ride it for kilometres.
54125.m: The pororoca is a tidal wave that runs up the Amazon.

54126.q: Which large tributary with almost black water meets the Amazon at Manaus?
54126.e: The Rio Negro has dark, acidic water that looks like tea because of dissolved plant matter. At Manaus it flows for kilometres beside the light, muddy water of the main river.
54126.m: The Rio Negro brings dark water into the Amazon.

54127.q: What lies in the huge mouth of the Amazon?
a: A river island about the size of Switzerland
54127.e: The island of Marajó lies in the mouth of the Amazon. At about 40,000 km², it is roughly the size of Switzerland.
54127.m: In the mouth of the Amazon lies an island as big as Switzerland.

54128.q: Which country did the first Europeans come from who travelled down the Amazon to its mouth in 1542?
54128.e: The Spanish conquistador Francisco de Orellana and his men travelled down the whole river from the Andes to the Atlantic.
54128.m: In 1542 Spaniards were the first Europeans to travel down the Amazon.

54129.q: Where does the river Amazon get its name from?
a: From women warriors in a Greek legend
From a chief of the native people
54129.e: Spanish explorers reported battles with armed women. They compared them with the Amazons, warrior women from Greek legend.
54129.m: The Amazon is named after the Amazons of Greek legend.

54130.q: Which large city lies at the tip of the Nile Delta, where the Nile divides?
54130.e: North of Cairo the Nile splits into two large branches. Between them lies the triangular, fertile Nile Delta.
54130.m: Cairo lies at the tip of the Nile Delta.

54131.q: Which large port city lies on the western edge of the Nile Delta?
54131.e: Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great and lies on the Mediterranean coast west of the delta. Today it is the second largest city in Egypt.
54131.m: Alexandria is the large port city on the edge of the Nile Delta.

54132.q: Which famous find from the Nile Delta helped decipher hieroglyphs in 1822?
54132.e: The Rosetta Stone carries the same text in hieroglyphs, in demotic script and in Greek. With it, Jean-François Champollion was able to decipher the hieroglyphs.
54132.m: A stone with three scripts from the Nile Delta helped people read hieroglyphs.

54133.q: Why has the coast of the Nile Delta been worn away in many places since the Aswan High Dam was built?
a: Because hardly any silt reaches the sea any more
Because the Nile flows much faster today
Because more rain falls in the delta than before
Because farmers dig up the soil
54133.e: Today the silt stays in the reservoir behind the dam. Without new silt, the sea can wear away the coast without new land building up.
54133.m: Without Nile silt, the delta no longer grows but gets smaller.

54134.q: Which danger from climate change threatens the very flat Nile Delta in particular?
54134.e: Large parts of the delta lie only a few metres above the sea. If sea levels rise, there is a risk of flooding and salty groundwater in the fields.
54134.m: Rising sea levels threaten the flat Nile Delta.

54135.q: Why is a river mouth with many branches called a “delta”?
a: It looks like a Greek letter
A scientist called Delta discovered it
54135.e: The triangular shape of the Nile's mouth reminded even the ancient Greeks of the capital letter delta, which looks like a triangle: Δ.
54135.m: The delta is named after a triangular Greek letter.

54136.q: Which fibre plant has been grown in large quantities in the Nile Delta since the 19th century?
54136.e: Egyptian cotton has especially long fibres and is considered very high quality. The fertile soil and irrigation in the delta are ideal for growing it.
54136.m: Famous Egyptian cotton grows in the Nile Delta.

54137.q: What is the section of a river near its source, where it usually flows steeply and fast, called?
54137.e: In the upper course the slope is steep and the water is fast. It wears away a lot of rock there and often cuts narrow valleys.
54137.m: In its upper course a river flows steeply and fast.

54138.q: How do you decide which bank of a river is the left one and which is the right one?
a: You look in the direction of flow
54138.e: Left and right banks are always named looking downstream. That way the names are clear all over the world.
54138.m: Left and right banks are named looking in the direction of flow.

54139.q: At which town does the Inn flow into the Danube?
54139.e: The Inn flows from the Engadine through Tyrol and Bavaria. In Passau, the City of Three Rivers, it joins the Danube.
54139.m: The Inn flows into the Danube at Passau.

54140.q: Which two streams join at Donaueschingen to form the Danube?
54140.e: The Brigach and Breg rise in the Black Forest and join at Donaueschingen. A German rhyme says that Brigach and Breg “bring the Danube about”.
54140.m: The Brigach and Breg together form the Danube.

54141.q: From which mountain lake near the Oberalp Pass does the Vorderrhein flow?
54141.e: Lake Toma (Lai da Tuma in Romansh) lies at over 2300 m. It is considered the source of the Vorderrhein and therefore of the Rhine.
54141.m: Lake Toma is considered the source of the Rhine.

54142.q: What is special about the point where the Aare flows into the Rhine at Koblenz AG?
a: The Aare carries more water than the Rhine
The Aare forms a large delta there
The Aare plunges over a waterfall there
54142.e: At the confluence the Aare carries on average about 485 m³ of water per second, the Rhine only about 440 m³. Even so, the river keeps the name Rhine afterwards.
54142.m: At Koblenz AG the Aare brings more water than the Rhine itself.

54143.q: When is a river more likely to form a delta than an estuary at its mouth?
a: When it brings a lot of material and the tides are weak
When it brings little material and the tides are strong
When it flows through high mountains
54143.e: A delta grows when a lot of sand and mud is deposited and the sea does not wash it away. With strong tides the material is carried off and the mouth widens into a funnel.
54143.m: A delta forms when a lot of mud stays put and the tides are weak.

54144.q: What is the technical term for a funnel-shaped river mouth?
54144.e: An estuary is a wide, funnel-shaped river mouth where the tides reach far inland. Fresh water and salt water mix there.
54144.m: A funnel-shaped river mouth is called an estuary.

54145.q: Which German river flows into the North Sea at Cuxhaven through a wide estuary?
54145.e: Below Hamburg the Elbe widens into a broad funnel. The strong North Sea tides reach far upstream.
54145.m: The Elbe has an estuary on the North Sea.

54146.q: What is the large wetland in the Rhone delta in southern France called?
54146.e: The Camargue lies between the branches of the Rhone where it meets the Mediterranean. It is known for white horses, black bulls and flamingos.
54146.m: The Camargue is the delta of the Rhone.

54147.q: Which river forms a protected delta, the Bolle di Magadino, on Lake Maggiore?
54147.e: The river Ticino deposits a lot of material in Lake Maggiore near Magadino. The Bolle di Magadino are an important nature reserve for birds.
54147.m: The Ticino forms a delta in Lake Maggiore.

54148.q: Which river forms the largest river delta in Europe?
54148.e: Before it reaches the sea, the Volga splits into hundreds of branches. Its delta is about 150 km wide and the largest in Europe.
54148.m: The Volga has the largest delta in Europe.

54149.q: What is meant by a river's drainage basin?
a: The whole area from which water flows into it
The stretch from the source to the mouth
The area flooded at high water
54149.e: The drainage basin includes every area from which rain and meltwater reach the river via streams and tributaries. The bigger it is, the more water a river can carry.
54149.m: The drainage basin is the whole area that drains into a river.

54150.q: Roughly how big is the drainage basin of the Amazon?
54150.e: The Amazon's drainage basin covers about 6 to 7 million km², almost as much as the whole of Australia. It is the largest drainage basin on Earth.
54150.m: The Amazon's drainage basin is about 7 million square kilometres.

54151.q: Roughly what part of Switzerland's area drains via the Rhine into the North Sea?
54151.e: About 68 per cent of Switzerland's area belongs to the Rhine's drainage basin. The rest drains via the Rhone, Po, Adige and Inn into other seas.
54151.m: About two thirds of Switzerland drains via the Rhine into the North Sea.

54152.q: What do you call an area from which no water flows out to the sea?
54152.e: In an endorheic basin the water ends up in a lake or seeps away and evaporates. Examples are the area around the Caspian Sea and the Dead Sea.
54152.m: No water flows from an endorheic basin to the sea.

54153.q: Which of these Swiss rivers belongs to the Rhine's drainage basin?
54153.e: The Aare flows into the Rhine at Koblenz AG. The Ticino flows to the Po, the Rhone into the Mediterranean and the Inn to the Danube.
54153.m: The Aare belongs to the Rhine's drainage basin.

54154.q: Which river has the largest drainage basin in Europe?
54154.e: The Volga's drainage basin covers about 1.36 million km² and lies almost entirely in Russia. That is more than thirty times the area of Switzerland.
54154.m: The Volga has the largest drainage basin in Europe.

54155.q: Which sea does water from Ticino reach via the river Po?
54155.e: The river Ticino flows through Lake Maggiore and into the Po. The Po flows into the Adriatic, part of the Mediterranean.
54155.m: Water from Ticino flows via the Po into the Adriatic.

54156.q: Where does a watershed usually run in the mountains?
54156.e: Water flows down from a ridge on both sides. That is why watersheds in the mountains usually follow the highest ridges.
54156.m: In the mountains the watershed usually runs along the ridges.

54157.q: Which mountain near Maloja is a triple watershed between the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea?
54157.e: From the area of Piz Lunghin, water flows via the Rhine into the North Sea, via the Po into the Adriatic and via the Inn and the Danube into the Black Sea.
54157.m: At Piz Lunghin the water divides between three seas.

54158.q: Which Alpine pass lies on the watershed between the Reuss and the Ticino?
54158.e: North of the Gotthard Pass the water flows via the Reuss into the Rhine. To the south it flows via the Ticino into the Po.
54158.m: The Gotthard Pass divides the waters of the Reuss and the Ticino.

54159.q: What is the line called that separates Europe's rivers flowing to the North Sea and Atlantic from those flowing to the Mediterranean and Black Sea?
54159.e: The European Watershed runs right across the continent and also through Switzerland. It crosses many Alpine passes and the Jura.
54159.m: The European Watershed separates the great seas of Europe.

54160.q: Which rivers all rise in the Gotthard area?
54160.e: The sources of the Rhine, Rhone, Reuss and Ticino lie in the Gotthard area. Their water flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean and, via the Po, the Adriatic.
54160.m: The Rhine, Rhone, Reuss and Ticino rise in the Gotthard area.

54161.q: Which pass between the Engadine and the Bregaglia lies on the watershed between the Inn and the Mera?
54161.e: On the Engadine side of the Maloja Pass the water flows into the Inn. On the steep Bregaglia side it flows via the Mera to Lake Como.
54161.m: The Maloja Pass divides the waters of the Inn and the Mera.

a: A branch of a river in a delta
54162.e: Meanders are bends and loops that a river forms on a plain. From above, the river then looks like a winding snake.
54162.m: A meander is a loop in a river.

54163.q: Where does the meander get its name from?
a: From a river in what is now Turkey
54163.e: The ancient river Maiandros, today the Büyük Menderes in Turkey, flows in many loops. All such river loops were named after it.
54163.m: The meander is named after a river in Turkey.

54164.q: What is the steep bank on the outside of a river bend called?
54164.e: On the outside of the bend the water flows faster and hits the bank. There the ground is worn away and the bank becomes steep.
54164.m: At the cut bank the river wears away the bank.

54165.q: What happens on the gentle slip-off slope on the inside of a river bend?
a: The bank is strongly worn away
54165.e: On the inside of the bend the water flows slowly. So material is left behind there and flat banks of sand and gravel form.
54165.m: On the slip-off slope the river deposits sand and gravel.

54166.q: What do you call a cut-off river loop in which the water is almost still?
54166.e: During a flood a river can break through the neck of a loop. The old loop is left behind as an oxbow lake and is a valuable habitat.
54166.m: An oxbow lake is a loop cut off from the river.

54167.q: What is the famous horseshoe-shaped loop of the Colorado River in Arizona called?
54167.e: At Horseshoe Bend the Colorado River winds deep in a canyon almost all the way round a rock. The place is a popular spot for photos.
54167.m: Horseshoe Bend is a river loop shaped like a horseshoe.

54168.q: Which river forms a large loop near Saint-Ursanne in the canton of Jura?
54168.e: The Doubs briefly flows into Switzerland, makes a wide loop near Saint-Ursanne and then returns to France. The landscape is called the Clos du Doubs.
54168.m: The Doubs makes a large loop in the Jura.

54169.q: What is the largest of the Niagara Falls, most of which belongs to Canada, called?
54169.e: Niagara Falls consists of three falls. The horseshoe-shaped Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side carry most of the water.
54169.m: The Horseshoe Falls are the largest part of Niagara Falls.

54170.q: Roughly how high is Angel Falls, the highest waterfall on Earth?
54170.e: Angel Falls plunges about 979 m, more than 800 m of it in free fall. It drops from a table mountain in Venezuela.
54170.m: Angel Falls is almost a kilometre high.

54171.q: Which waterfalls in the Lauterbrunnen valley plunge down inside a mountain?
54171.e: The Trümmelbach has carved a gorge into the rock and plunges in several steps through the mountain. It brings meltwater from the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
54171.m: The Trümmelbach Falls thunder inside a mountain.

54172.q: Which river forms the Khone Falls in Laos, considered the widest waterfalls in the world?
54172.e: The Khone Falls spread over more than 10 km with many steps and islands. They stop ships from travelling the whole river.
54172.m: In Laos the Mekong forms the very wide Khone Falls.

54173.q: What is the famous waterfall in Iceland whose name means “golden waterfall”?
54173.e: Gullfoss plunges in two steps into a deep gorge of the river Hvítá. It is one of the best-known sights in Iceland.

54174.q: Which waterfall in South Africa is often considered the second highest on Earth?
54174.e: The Tugela Falls in the Drakensberg mountains plunge about 950 m in several steps. Only Angel Falls is considered higher.
54174.m: The Tugela Falls are among the highest waterfalls on Earth.

54175.q: How does a waterfall often form?
a: Soft rock under hard rock is worn away faster
An earthquake lifts the riverbed every year
The river freezes and thaws again
54175.e: When a hard layer of rock lies above softer rock, the soft rock below is washed out. The hard edge remains as a step and the water plunges over it.
54175.m: Waterfalls often form at a step of hard rock.

54176.q: Which larger river does the Iguazú flow into shortly after its waterfalls?
54176.e: After the falls, the Iguazú flows on for about 20 km and then joins the Paraná. There the borders of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay meet.
54176.m: The Iguazú flows into the Paraná.

54177.q: Roughly how wide is the edge of the Iguazú Falls in total?
54177.e: The falls spread along an edge about 2.7 km long in the shape of a horseshoe. Between them lie islands with rainforest.
54177.m: The Iguazú Falls are almost three kilometres wide.

54179.q: Apart from the falls themselves, what do the national parks at the Iguazú Falls protect?
54179.e: The national parks in Argentina and Brazil protect the falls and the rainforest with its many animals. Both have been UNESCO World Natural Heritage Sites since the 1980s.
54179.m: At the Iguazú Falls the rainforest is protected too.

54180.q: Roughly how high are the Iguazú Falls at their highest points?
54180.e: Most of the falls drop about 60 to 80 m, the highest up to about 82 m. So they are much wider than they are high.
54180.m: The Iguazú Falls are up to about 80 metres high.

54181.q: Which Brazilian town lies close to the Iguazú Falls?
54181.e: Foz do Iguaçu lies in southern Brazil where it meets Argentina and Paraguay. From here many travellers visit the Brazilian side of the falls.
54181.m: Foz do Iguaçu is the Brazilian town near the Iguazú Falls.

54182.q: On which side of the border does the larger part of the Iguazú Falls lie?
54182.e: Most of the individual falls are in Argentina. From the Brazilian side, however, you get a good view of their whole width.
54182.m: The larger part of the Iguazú Falls lies in Argentina.

54183.q: Which lake is the largest lake in Europe?
54183.e: Lake Ladoga lies in Russia, north-east of St Petersburg, and covers about 17,700 km². That makes it almost half the size of Switzerland.
54183.m: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe.

54184.q: Which lake is the second largest in Europe after Lake Ladoga?
54184.e: Lake Onega also lies in north-west Russia and covers almost 10,000 km². It is connected to Lake Ladoga by rivers and canals.
54184.m: Lake Onega is the second largest lake in Europe.

54185.q: Which lake is considered the highest navigable lake on Earth?
54185.e: Lake Titicaca lies at about 3810 m above sea level in the Andes. Ships and boats made of reeds sail on it.
54185.m: Lake Titicaca is the highest navigable lake in the world.

54186.q: Roughly how many times bigger than Switzerland is the Caspian Sea?
54186.e: The Caspian Sea covers about 370,000 to 390,000 km². Switzerland measures about 41,000 km².
54186.m: The Caspian Sea is about nine times the size of Switzerland.

54187.q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely in Canada?
54187.e: Great Bear Lake lies in the Northwest Territories near the Arctic Circle and covers more than 31,000 km². It is frozen for many months of the year.
54187.m: Great Bear Lake is the largest lake entirely in Canada.

54188.q: Which large salt lake in Australia is almost dried out most of the time?
54188.e: Lake Eyre, also called Kati Thanda, is the largest lake in Australia. It only fills with water after rare heavy rainfall.
54188.m: Lake Eyre in Australia is usually dried out.

54189.q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland?
54189.e: Lake Neuchâtel covers about 218 km² and lies completely in Switzerland. Switzerland shares Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Maggiore with neighbouring countries.
54189.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely in Switzerland.

54190.q: Which lake is the largest freshwater lake on Earth by area?
54190.e: Lake Superior lies in North America on the border between Canada and the USA. No other freshwater lake has a larger surface area.
54190.m: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake on Earth by area.

54191.q: How big is Lake Superior compared with Switzerland?
54191.e: Lake Superior covers about 82,000 km², Switzerland about 41,000 km². So it is about twice as big.
54191.m: Lake Superior is about twice the size of Switzerland.

54192.q: Which Canadian province borders Lake Superior?
54192.e: The whole northern shore of Lake Superior belongs to the province of Ontario. On the southern shore lie the US states of Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan.
54192.m: The Canadian province of Ontario lies on Lake Superior.

54194.q: Why can Lake Superior be dangerous for large ships?
a: Because of violent autumn storms with high waves
54194.e: In autumn, heavy storms with waves several metres high often rage on Lake Superior. In 1975 the cargo ship Edmund Fitzgerald sank there and all 29 sailors died.
54194.m: Autumn storms make Lake Superior dangerous.

54195.q: Which animals is the island of Isle Royale in Lake Superior famous for?
54195.e: Isle Royale is a US national park. For decades scientists have studied how wolves and moose live together there.
54195.m: Wolves and moose live on Isle Royale.

54196.q: How do ships overcome the difference in height between Lake Superior and Lake Huron?
54196.e: Lake Superior lies about 6 to 7 metres higher than Lake Huron. At Sault Ste. Marie, locks raise and lower the ships.
54196.m: Locks connect Lake Superior with Lake Huron.

54197.q: Roughly how deep is Lake Superior at its deepest point?
54197.e: The deepest point of Lake Superior is about 406 m below the surface. It is the deepest of the five Great Lakes.
54197.m: Lake Superior is up to about 400 metres deep.

54198.q: Which record does Lake Tanganyika hold among the freshwater lakes of the world?
a: It is the largest by area
54198.e: Lake Tanganyika is about 670 km long but usually only 50 km wide. No other freshwater lake is as long.
54198.m: Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake in the world.

54199.q: How many countries border Lake Tanganyika?
54199.e: Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi and Zambia lie on its shores. Most of it belongs to Tanzania and the Congo.
54199.m: Four countries share the shores of Lake Tanganyika.

54200.q: Which missing explorer did Henry Morton Stanley find at Lake Tanganyika in 1871?
54200.e: Stanley had searched for Livingstone for a long time. In the village of Ujiji he is said to have greeted him with the famous words “Dr Livingstone, I presume?”
54200.m: Stanley met Livingstone at Lake Tanganyika in 1871.

54201.q: Which fish is Lake Tanganyika famous for among scientists and aquarium keepers?
54201.e: About 250 species of cichlid live in Lake Tanganyika, most of them found nowhere else. They developed over a long time in this very old lake.
54201.m: Lake Tanganyika is famous for its many cichlid species.

54202.q: How did the deep basin of Lake Tanganyika form?
a: Through a rift where the Earth's crust is drifting apart
54202.e: The lake lies in the East African Rift. There the Earth's crust is tearing apart and the ground sinks between steep edges.
54202.m: Lake Tanganyika lies in a rift in the Earth's crust.

54203.q: In which part of Africa does Lake Tanganyika lie?
a: In the north, on the Mediterranean
In the west, on the Atlantic
In the far south, at the Cape
54203.e: Lake Tanganyika lies in East Africa in the East African Rift. Tanzania, the Congo, Burundi and Zambia lie on its shores.
54203.m: Lake Tanganyika lies in East Africa.

54204.q: What were the British explorers looking for who, in 1858, were the first Europeans to reach Lake Tanganyika?
54204.e: Richard Burton and John Speke were searching for the sources of the Nile. On the way, they reached Lake Tanganyika in 1858.
54204.m: Explorers searched East Africa for a long time for the sources of the Nile.

a: A lake that has been artificially created by a dam
A lake without an outflow in the desert
A lake formed by a glacier
A lake in a volcanic crater
54205.e: For a reservoir, a wall or dam blocks off a valley. The water is used for electricity, irrigation, drinking water or flood protection.
54205.m: A reservoir forms behind an artificial dam.

54206.q: What are most reservoirs in the Swiss Alps used for?
54206.e: Water from the reservoirs flows through pipes to power stations in the valley, where it drives turbines. Hydropower supplies about 60 per cent of Switzerland's electricity.
54206.m: Alpine reservoirs supply electricity from hydropower.

54207.q: Which lake is the largest reservoir in Switzerland by area?
54207.e: The Sihlsee near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz covers about 11 km². It was dammed in the 1930s to generate electricity.
54207.m: The Sihlsee is the largest reservoir in Switzerland by area.

54208.q: Which huge hydroelectric power station on the border between Brazil and Paraguay is one of the most powerful in the world?
54208.e: The Itaipú power station supplies a large part of the electricity for Paraguay and Brazil. Only a few power stations in the world produce more electricity.
54208.m: Itaipú is one of the largest hydroelectric power stations in the world.

54209.q: Which desert city gets a lot of water from the reservoir behind the Hoover Dam?
54209.e: Lake Mead lies behind the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River. It supplies desert cities such as Las Vegas with water.
54209.m: The Hoover Dam supplies Las Vegas with water.

54210.q: What disadvantage do dams have for many fish such as salmon and trout?
a: They heat the water to over 40 degrees
They put too much oxygen into the water
54210.e: Many fish swim upstream to spawn. They can only get past a dam wall using special fish ladders, or not at all.
54210.m: Dams block the way for migrating fish.

54211.q: What is the structure called that safely carries surplus water past a dam during a flood?
54211.e: When a reservoir is full and even more water flows in, it must be able to flow away in a controlled way. Otherwise the water could spill over the wall and damage the dam.
54211.m: The spillway protects a dam from too much water.

a: The highest mountains of the seven continents
The seven highest mountains of the Alps
The seven highest volcanoes on Earth
Seven peaks in the Himalayas over 8000 m
54212.e: The “Seven Summits” are the highest mountain on each of the seven continents.
54212.m: The Seven Summits are the highest peaks of all seven continents.

54213.q: Which mountain is the highest in Africa and one of the Seven Summits?
54213.e: Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with its summit Kibo, is about 5895 m high. It is the highest mountain in Africa.
54213.m: Kilimanjaro is the roof of Africa.

54214.q: Which mountain is counted as the highest in Europe in most lists of the Seven Summits?
54214.e: Elbrus in the Caucasus in Russia is about 5642 m high. Because the Caucasus is usually counted as part of Europe, it is considered Europe's highest peak; otherwise it would be Mont Blanc.
54214.m: Elbrus in the Caucasus is usually counted as the highest mountain in Europe.

54215.q: On which continent is Mount Everest, the highest of the Seven Summits?
54215.e: Mount Everest lies in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and China. At about 8849 m, it is the highest mountain on Earth.
54215.m: Mount Everest in Asia is the highest of the Seven Summits.

54216.q: Which mountain is the highest in South America and one of the Seven Summits?
54216.e: Aconcagua in the Andes in Argentina is about 6960 m high. It is the highest mountain outside Asia.
54216.m: Aconcagua is the highest mountain in South America.

54217.q: What makes climbing the highest of the Seven Summits especially difficult?
a: The air contains very little oxygen
There are too many trees there
The ground is as soft as sand
54217.e: The higher you climb, the thinner the air becomes. On Mount Everest you get only about a third as much oxygen with each breath as at sea level.
54217.m: At high altitude the air is thin and low in oxygen.

54218.q: Which of the Seven Summits is in North America?
54218.e: Denali in Alaska is about 6190 m high. It used to be called Mount McKinley.
54218.m: Denali is the highest mountain in North America.

54219.q: On the border between which two countries does Mount Everest lie?
54219.e: The summit of Mount Everest lies exactly on the border between Nepal and China. On the Chinese side lies the region of Tibet.
54219.m: Mount Everest lies on the border of Nepal and China.

54220.q: Why is the Khumbu Icefall on Mount Everest so dangerous?
a: Ice towers collapse and crevasses open up
54220.e: In the Khumbu Icefall the glacier is constantly moving. Ice towers can suddenly collapse and new crevasses can open up. It lies just above the base camp.
54220.m: The Khumbu Icefall is one of the most dangerous places on Everest.

54221.q: George Mallory disappeared on Mount Everest in 1924. Which mystery remains unsolved to this day?
a: Whether he was ever in Nepal
54221.e: Mallory and Andrew Irvine were last seen high on the north-east ridge in 1924. Mallory was not found until 1999. Nobody knows whether the two reached the summit.
54221.m: Whether Mallory reached the summit in 1924 remains a mystery.

54222.q: How high is Everest Base Camp compared with the Alps?
a: About as high as the Säntis
About as high as Lake Zurich
Higher than the summit of Everest
54222.e: The base camp in Nepal lies at about 5300 to 5400 metres. The highest mountain in the Alps, Mont Blanc, is only about 4800 metres high.
54222.m: Even Everest Base Camp is higher than any Alpine peak.

54224.q: What did Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler achieve first on Mount Everest in 1978?
54224.e: On 8 May 1978 Messner and Habeler reached the summit without oxygen bottles. Before that, many people thought this was impossible.
54224.m: In 1978 Messner and Habeler climbed Everest without bottled oxygen.

54225.q: Which expedition made the second ascent of Mount Everest in 1956?
54225.e: The Swiss climbers Ernst Schmied and Jürg Marmet stood on the summit in May 1956, later followed by Dölf Reist and Hansruedi von Gunten. The same expedition made the first ascent of Lhotse.
54225.m: Swiss climbers made the second ascent of Everest in 1956.

54226.q: Why do most climbers on Everest need oxygen bottles?
a: The air contains very little oxygen
The wind blows the oxygen away
The ice uses up the oxygen
54226.e: At about 8800 m the air pressure is only about a third of what it is at sea level. So you get much less oxygen with every breath.
54226.m: The higher you climb, the less oxygen you get with every breath.

a: Through the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate
Through a fall in sea level
54227.e: The Indian Plate has been pushing against the Eurasian Plate for about 50 million years. This piled up the rock into a huge fold mountain range.
54227.m: The Himalayas are fold mountains formed by two colliding plates.

54228.q: Which shaggy type of cattle is kept as a pack animal in the Himalayas?
54228.e: The yak has thick, long fur and copes well with cold and thin air. It carries loads and provides milk, wool and meat.
54228.m: The yak is the pack animal of the Himalayas.

54229.q: What do climbers call the area above about 7500 to 8000 m, where the body can no longer recover?
54229.e: At this height the body gets so little oxygen that it breaks down, even at rest. Climbers therefore try to stay there only briefly.
54229.m: In the death zone the body keeps breaking down because of a lack of oxygen.

54230.q: Who was the first person to climb all the eight-thousanders?
54230.e: Reinhold Messner from South Tyrol completed the series in 1986 with Lhotse. Shortly afterwards the Polish climber Jerzy Kukuczka followed.
54230.m: In 1986 Reinhold Messner became the first to stand on all 14 eight-thousanders.

54231.q: What is the mountain people of Nepal called whose members often work as porters and guides in the Himalayas?
54231.e: The Sherpas live in the high valleys of Nepal and are used to the thin air. Many accompany expeditions to the high peaks.
54231.m: Sherpas are experienced mountain guides in the Himalayas.

54232.q: Which holy river of India rises at a glacier in the Himalayas?
54232.e: The Ganges rises at the Gangotri Glacier in the Indian Himalayas. It flows through northern India and Bangladesh into the Bay of Bengal.
54232.m: The Ganges begins as a glacier stream in the Himalayas.

54233.q: Where does K2 rank among the highest mountains on Earth?
54233.e: K2 is about 8611 m high. Only Mount Everest is higher.
54233.m: K2 is the second highest mountain in the world.

54234.q: In which mountain range does K2 lie?
54234.e: K2 lies in the Karakoram on the border between Pakistan and China. The Karakoram is a separate range north-west of the Himalayas.
54234.m: K2 is the highest mountain in the Karakoram.

54235.q: Where does the unusual name “K2” come from?
a: From a survey number in the Karakoram
54235.e: In 1856 a British surveyor numbered the peaks in the Karakoram K1, K2 and so on. No other name caught on for K2.
54235.m: K2 simply means peak number 2 in the Karakoram.

54236.q: Which country did the first climbers of K2 come from in 1954?
54236.e: Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli of an Italian expedition reached the summit on 31 July 1954.
54236.m: K2 was first climbed by Italians in 1954.

54237.q: Why is K2 considered one of the most dangerous mountains in the world?
a: It is very steep and the weather changes quickly
It stands in the middle of a desert
54237.e: K2 is also called the “Savage Mountain”. Many climbers have died on it.
54237.m: Because of its dangers, K2 is called the savage mountain.

54238.q: Which team made the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021?
54238.e: Ten Nepali climbers, including Nirmal Purja, reached the summit together on 16 January 2021. K2 was the last eight-thousander without a winter ascent.
54238.m: Nepali climbers were the first to conquer K2 in winter, in 2021.

54239.q: Which two countries meet at the summit of K2?
54239.e: The border between Pakistan and China runs over the summit. Most expeditions start from the Pakistani side.
54239.m: K2 stands on the border between Pakistan and China.

54240.e: Aconcagua lies in the province of Mendoza in Argentina, near the border with Chile.

54241.q: In which mountain range is Aconcagua?
54241.e: The Andes stretch for about 7500 km along the west coast of South America. Aconcagua is their highest peak.
54241.m: Aconcagua is the highest peak of the Andes.

54242.e: Aconcagua is about 6961 m high. That makes it the highest mountain outside Asia.
54242.m: No mountain outside Asia is higher than Aconcagua.

54243.q: Where did Matthias Zurbriggen, the first person to stand on Aconcagua in 1897, come from?
54243.e: The mountain guide Matthias Zurbriggen was born in Saas-Fee in Valais and grew up in Macugnaga in Piedmont. He reached the summit on 14 January 1897 on a British expedition.
54243.m: Mountain guide Matthias Zurbriggen, born in Saas-Fee, was the first to stand on Aconcagua in 1897.

a: Highest mountain in the Southern Hemisphere
54244.e: No mountain south of the equator and none in the Western Hemisphere is higher than Aconcagua. It is not considered an active volcano.
54244.m: Aconcagua is the highest mountain in the Southern Hemisphere.

54245.q: Which of these mountains is higher than Aconcagua?
54245.e: Aconcagua is about 6961 m high. Only mountains in Asia, such as Mount Everest at 8849 m, are higher.
54245.m: Only mountains in Asia are higher than Aconcagua.

54246.q: Why is Aconcagua dangerous even though its normal route is easy?
a: Because of thin air, cold and strong winds
Because of deep crevasses at the summit
54246.e: At almost 7000 m the air has very little oxygen, and storms bring great cold. Many climbers underestimate altitude sickness.
54246.m: Even a technically easy high peak can be dangerous because of the altitude.

54247.q: In which US state is Denali?
54247.e: Denali lies in the Alaska Range in Denali National Park. It is the highest mountain in North America.
54247.m: The highest mountain in North America stands in Alaska.

54248.q: Which mountain is the highest in North America?
54248.e: Denali in Alaska is about 6190 metres high. Aconcagua in South America is higher, but it is on a different continent.
54248.m: Denali is the highest mountain in North America.

54249.q: By what other name is Denali also known?
54249.e: The native people of Alaska called the mountain Denali, “the high one”. The US government officially named it Denali in 2015, but renamed it Mount McKinley again in 2025 (as of 2025).
54249.m: Denali is also called Mount McKinley.

a: Greatest rise from base to summit on land
Highest mountain in the Northern Hemisphere
54250.e: Denali rises about 5500 m above the surrounding lowlands. No other mountain standing entirely on land rises so high above its surroundings.
54250.m: Denali rises enormously above the flat land around it.

54251.q: What covers large parts of Denali all year round?
54251.e: Denali is more than 6000 metres high and lies far to the north. That is why there is snow and huge glaciers there all year round.
54251.m: Denali is covered in glaciers all year round.

54252.q: Why is it especially cold on Denali?
a: It is high and far to the north
It is surrounded by sea ice
54252.e: Denali lies close to the Arctic Circle and is more than 6000 m high. So temperatures below minus 40 degrees are possible there.
54252.m: Height and nearness to the Arctic Circle make Denali icy cold.

54253.q: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?
a: A belt of volcanoes around the Pacific
A chain of bushfires in Australia
A ring of coral reefs in the Pacific
An ocean current off South America
54253.e: The Ring of Fire is a belt about 40,000 km long around the Pacific Ocean. There are especially many volcanoes and earthquakes there.
54253.m: A belt of volcanoes and earthquakes runs around the Pacific.

54254.q: Roughly what share of the Earth's active and dormant volcanoes lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire?
54254.e: About 75 per cent of the Earth's active and dormant volcanoes lie on the Ring of Fire. About 90 per cent of all earthquakes also happen there.
54254.m: Most of the Earth's volcanoes lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire.

54255.q: Which process causes most of the volcanoes on the Pacific Ring of Fire?
a: A meteorite tore open the crust
Glaciers press down on the crust
54255.e: The Pacific Plate and other plates sink beneath neighbouring plates. This sinking is called subduction; rock melts and magma forms.
54255.m: On the Ring of Fire plates sink down, creating volcanoes and earthquakes.

54256.q: Which active volcano lies only about 70 km from Mexico City?
54256.e: Popocatépetl is about 5400 m high and one of the most active volcanoes in Mexico. Its name comes from the Aztec language Nahuatl and means “smoking mountain”.
54256.m: Popocatépetl is the smoking mountain near Mexico City.

54257.q: Which volcano in the US state of Washington erupted in 1980 and lost part of its summit?
54257.e: On 18 May 1980 the north side of Mount St. Helens slid away, followed by a huge sideways explosion. The mountain became about 400 m lower.
54257.m: Mount St. Helens exploded sideways in 1980 and became much lower.

54258.q: Which volcano in Ecuador is one of the highest active volcanoes on Earth?
54258.e: Cotopaxi in the Andes of Ecuador is about 5900 m high and has a cap of glaciers. It lies on the eastern edge of the Pacific Ring of Fire.
54258.m: Cotopaxi in Ecuador is a high, glacier-covered volcano.

54259.q: Which city in California was largely destroyed in 1906 by an earthquake and the fires that followed?
54259.e: The earthquake on the San Andreas Fault shook San Francisco in April 1906. The fires that followed destroyed a large part of the city.
54259.m: San Francisco was devastated by an earthquake and fires in 1906.

54260.q: Which country is NOT part of the Pacific Ring of Fire?
54260.e: Iceland lies in the North Atlantic and gets its volcanoes from a different plate boundary. Japan, New Zealand and Indonesia all lie on the edge of the Pacific.
54260.m: Not every volcanic country lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire.

54261.q: What is a composite volcano made of?
a: Alternating layers of lava and ash
54261.e: With each eruption, new layers of solidified lava and loose material such as ash are deposited. So the mountain grows layer by layer.
54261.m: A composite volcano grows from many layers of lava and ash.

54262.q: What shape does a typical composite volcano have?
a: A long crack in the ground
54262.e: The thick lava does not flow far and hardens near the crater. That is why steep, high cones form.
54262.m: Composite volcanoes are usually steep cones.

54263.q: How do composite volcanoes usually erupt?
a: Explosively, because the thick lava traps gases
Not at all, they are extinct
54263.e: Thick, sticky lava does not let gases escape easily, so pressure builds up. This is often released in violent explosions with ash.
54263.m: Thick lava makes volcanic eruptions especially explosive.

54264.q: What is another name for a composite volcano?
54264.e: The Latin word “stratum” means layer. So stratovolcano is another name for a composite volcano.
54264.m: Stratovolcano is another word for composite volcano.

54265.q: Which composite volcano on an island north of Sicily is called the “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean”?
54265.e: For thousands of years Stromboli has been throwing out glowing lumps of lava every few minutes. At night sailors could see the glow from far away.
54265.m: Stromboli is the lighthouse of the Mediterranean.

54266.q: What shape does a shield volcano have?
54266.e: Shield volcanoes have gently rising slopes. Their name comes from looking like a warrior's shield lying on the ground.
54266.m: A shield volcano looks like a shield lying down.

54267.q: Which kind of lava builds up a shield volcano?
54267.e: Runny basalt lava flows a long way before it hardens. This creates wide volcanoes with gentle slopes.
54267.m: Runny lava builds flat shield volcanoes.

54268.q: How do eruptions of shield volcanoes usually happen?
a: Fairly calmly, with lava flowing out
54268.e: With runny lava, gases can escape easily. So the lava usually flows out calmly in streams, often with lava fountains.
54268.m: Shield volcanoes usually erupt calmly with lava flows.

54269.q: Which shield volcano on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system?
54269.e: Olympus Mons is about 22 km high, measured from the average level of the Martian surface. That is about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest above the sea.
54269.m: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the solar system.

54270.q: On which group of islands are the best-known shield volcanoes on Earth?
54270.e: The Hawaiian Islands consist of huge shield volcanoes that have grown up from the seabed. They lie above a hot spot in the Earth's mantle.
54270.m: Hawaii was formed from mighty shield volcanoes.

54271.q: Near which Italian city is Vesuvius?
54271.e: Vesuvius rises on the Bay of Naples in Campania. About three million people live in the area around it.
54271.m: Vesuvius towers over the Bay of Naples.

54272.q: Vesuvius has been quiet for decades. Why is it still closely monitored?
a: It is an active volcano and can erupt again
It could slide into the sea
There is a lot of gold on it
54272.e: Vesuvius last erupted in 1944. It is still considered an active volcano. Instruments watch for earthquakes and gases to spot an eruption early.
54272.m: Vesuvius is an active volcano that can erupt again.

54273.q: How do we know what happened during the eruption of Vesuvius in the year 79?
a: A Roman eyewitness described it in letters
54273.e: The Roman Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from a distance and later wrote letters about it. There are also the finds from Pompeii.
54273.m: A Roman eyewitness described the eruption of Vesuvius in 79.

54274.q: What makes Vesuvius especially dangerous today?
a: A great many people live right on its slopes
It lies in the middle of the sea
It is the highest volcano in Europe
54274.e: Around Vesuvius, villages and towns are built high up the mountain. So there are detailed evacuation plans for a large eruption.
54274.m: Because so many people live around it, Vesuvius is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes.

54275.q: Which type of volcano is Vesuvius, with its steep cone?
54275.e: Composite volcanoes are made of alternating layers of lava and ash. They are steep and often erupt explosively, like Vesuvius.
54275.m: Vesuvius is a steep composite volcano.

54276.q: What happened to Pompeii when Vesuvius erupted in the year 79?
a: The town was buried under ash and pumice
The town was split by an earthquake
The town sank into the sea
The town was washed away by lava
54276.e: Pompeii was covered by several metres of pumice and ash. Beneath it, the town stayed hidden for many centuries.
54276.m: Pompeii lay buried under volcanic ash for many centuries.

54277.q: Since which century has Pompeii been systematically excavated?
54277.e: The excavations began in 1748 under the Bourbon kings of Naples. Even today the whole town has not yet been uncovered.
54277.m: Pompeii has been excavated since the 18th century.

54278.q: How were the famous plaster casts of the victims of Pompeii made?
a: Plaster was poured into hollows in the ash
Roman artists shaped them after the eruption
The bodies turned to stone by themselves
They were found in a Roman museum
54278.e: The bodies decayed in the hardened ash and left hollow spaces. From 1863 the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli filled these with plaster.
54278.m: The plaster figures of Pompeii are casts of hollows in the ash.

54279.q: Why is Pompeii so valuable for historians?
a: It shows everyday Roman life as if frozen
It was the capital of the Roman Empire
The Latin alphabet was invented there
It is the oldest city in the world
54279.e: Houses, shops, wall paintings and even inscriptions were preserved under the ash. So you can see how people lived almost 2000 years ago.
54279.m: Pompeii is a window into the everyday life of the ancient Romans.

54280.q: Roughly what part of the island of Hawaii does Mauna Loa cover?
54280.e: Mauna Loa covers about 51 per cent of the area of the island of Hawaii (the Big Island). The island is made up of five volcanoes.
54280.m: Mauna Loa takes up about half of the island of Hawaii.

54281.q: What kind of mountain is Mauna Loa in Hawaii?
54281.e: Mauna Loa is one of the largest volcanoes on Earth. It is built from countless lava flows.
54281.m: Mauna Loa is a huge volcano.

54282.q: Why is Mauna Loa much higher if you measure it from the seabed?
a: Because it starts deep under water
Because it stands on a glacier
Because the sea is very shallow there
54282.e: Above the sea, Mauna Loa is about 4170 metres high. But its base lies thousands of metres down on the seabed.
54282.m: Most of Mauna Loa lies under the sea.

54283.q: What happened at Mauna Loa in Hawaii in 2022?
a: It was completely buried in snow
It was climbed for the first time
54283.e: At the end of November 2022 Mauna Loa erupted. Before that, the volcano had been quiet for 38 years.
54283.m: Mauna Loa is an active volcano.

54284.q: What has been measured at a station on Mauna Loa since 1958?
a: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air
The water temperature of the Pacific
54284.e: At the Mauna Loa Observatory the CO2 content of the air is measured. The curve of measurements, the Keeling Curve, shows the steady rise of this greenhouse gas.
54284.m: Since 1958 the rise of CO2 in the air has been measured on Mauna Loa.

54285.q: What is the neighbouring volcano in Hawaii that is higher than Mauna Loa called?
54285.e: Mauna Kea is about 4207 m high and so slightly higher. Measured from the seabed, it is more than 10,000 m high.
54285.m: Mauna Kea is the highest mountain in Hawaii.

54286.q: In which country is the volcano Krakatoa?
54286.e: Krakatoa lies in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra. Indonesia has more active volcanoes than almost any other country.
54286.m: Krakatoa lies in Indonesia between Java and Sumatra.

54287.q: In which year did the famous great eruption of Krakatoa happen?
54287.e: At the end of August 1883 the volcano exploded and most of the island disappeared. It was one of the most violent natural disasters of modern times.

54288.q: What caused the most deaths in the Krakatoa eruption of 1883?
54288.e: The eruption set off tsunamis that destroyed villages on the coasts of Java and Sumatra. In total about 36,000 people died.
54288.m: Most victims of the Krakatoa eruption died in tsunamis.

54289.q: What is especially remarkable about the Krakatoa eruption of 1883?
a: The bang could be heard thousands of kilometres away
The lava flowed as far as Australia
It lasted more than ten years
It was the first volcanic eruption ever
54289.e: The explosion could still be heard on the island of Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean, almost 5000 km away. It is considered one of the loudest sounds in history.
54289.m: The bang of Krakatoa is considered one of the loudest sounds in history.

54290.q: What does the name “Anak Krakatau”, the new volcano in the same place, mean?
54290.e: From 1927 a new volcano grew up out of the sea. The local people called it Anak Krakatau in Indonesian, “child of Krakatoa”.
54290.m: Anak Krakatau is the child of the old Krakatoa.

54291.q: What worldwide effect did the Krakatoa eruption of 1883 have?
a: A one-metre rise in sea level
A shift in the Earth's axis
54291.e: Fine ash and sulphur gases spread through the high atmosphere around the whole Earth. For months they turned evening skies a striking red and cooled the climate slightly.
54291.m: Volcanic ash in the atmosphere can turn the sky red all over the world.

54292.q: Why are there so many volcanoes in Iceland?
a: It lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
It lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire
It lies in the middle of an old plate
It was hit by a meteorite
54292.e: Iceland lies where the North American and Eurasian plates drift apart. In addition, especially hot mantle rock rises beneath Iceland.
54292.m: In Iceland two tectonic plates are drifting apart.

54293.q: Which Icelandic volcano brought air traffic in Europe to a standstill for days with its ash cloud in 2010?
54293.e: The ash from Eyjafjallajökull drifted over Europe and thousands of flights were cancelled. Planes stayed on the ground in Switzerland too.
54293.m: Eyjafjallajökull stopped air traffic in Europe in 2010.

54294.q: What happened off the coast of Iceland from 1963?
a: A new island grew out of the sea through a volcanic eruption
An island sank completely into the sea
A glacier slid into the sea
A meteorite crashed into the sea
54294.e: The island of Surtsey grew out of the sea between 1963 and 1967. Scientists watch there how plants and animals settle on new land.
54294.m: Surtsey is a young volcanic island off Iceland.

54295.q: What does Iceland mainly use the heat from underground for?
54295.e: Hot water from deep down is piped to the houses. About nine out of ten homes in Iceland are heated with geothermal energy in this way.
54295.m: Iceland heats most of its homes with geothermal energy.

54296.q: What can you see in Thingvellir National Park in Iceland?
a: The largest waterfall in the world
54296.e: In Thingvellir National Park you can see deep cracks in the rock where the North American and Eurasian plates drift apart.
54296.m: In Thingvellir you can see Iceland being pulled apart.

54297.q: What effect did a large volcanic eruption in Iceland in 1783 have in Europe?
54297.e: For eight months, lava and huge amounts of poisonous gases poured out of the Laki fissure. Many animals and people in Iceland died, and harvests in Europe suffered too.
54297.m: The Laki eruption of 1783 brought hunger to Iceland and Europe.

54298.q: What did many people in the Middle Ages believe about the Icelandic volcano Hekla?
a: That there was an entrance to hell there
That a gold treasure lay there
